title: Qld government reveals the cost of upgrading Brisbane's RNA showgrounds
text:
The state government is splashing almost $300 million dollars to upgrade Brisbane's RNA showgrounds ahead of the 2032 Games.

The 20,000-seat outdoor arena will be revitalised, including an upgraded Machinery Hill grandstand, multi-storey horse pavilion, and major accessibility improvements.

Construction on the Bowen Hills site will begin after this year's 150th edition of the Ekka, with the event to run uninterrupted until 2032.

The state government has previously refused to reveal the cost of the upgrades, citing it as commercial in confidence.

The Ekka will continue to be run at the site. (Supplied)

Deputy premier Jarrod Bleijie today claimed it had been brought in on budget.

"As I said a year ago, we were going to ensure things were going to be done on time and on budget," he said.

"I'm delighted to say that the $287.5 million was what was requested by the RNA.

"It is being delivered and contracted with Hutchinson Builders."

Loading...

The showgrounds upgrade is funded as part of the $3.5 billion investment into athletes' villages for the 2032 Brisbane Olympic and Paralympic Games.

A 2,000-unit village will overlook the arena, housing up to 10,000 athletes during the Games, to then be converted to housing.

Construction at the site last year marked the first works for any Olympic infrastructure, including restoration to two of the heritage listed grandstands.

Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie said the upgrade has come in on budget. (ABC News)

Accessibility improvements

RNA chief executive Brendan Christou said the upgrades would be vital to ensure the Ekka could continue for a further 150 years, particularly through accessibility.

"What our smart designers have done is create accessible pathways from the very high levels up on Brookes Street and O'Connell Terrace, right down to the main arena level, with multiple accessible pathways.

"That's going to be important for obviously the Paralympic athletes who are going to be housed up there in the new accommodation, but also for legacy."

Upgrades to the showgrounds will make them more accessible. (Supplied)

With a decreased amount of space available, he highlighted the innovation involved in the latest construction.

"Whilst the footprint has shrunk a little bit, we've actually gone vertical to create the same amount of square meters in event space," Mr Christou said.

"So the horse stables that currently exists that are in very poor condition, will be replaced by a multi-storey facility to house those horses."

The RNA announcement follows the weekend release of the Victoria Park masterplan, with two pedestrian bridges to link the Brisbane Stadium with the CBD and National Aquatic Centre.

The government was also tight-lipped on costs for the infrastructure, with the bridges and park development funds kept separate from the main $7.1 billion venues funding envelope.

title: Calls for tree felling regulation after man crushed at Buddhist monastery
text:
There are renewed calls for the regulation of private tree felling activities after a retired nurse was accidentally crushed to death at a Buddhist monastery.

An investigation by Coroner Leigh Mackey into the death of a man referred to as LO in November 2023 found the incident was "avoidable", with the "absence of training" a contributing factor.

"The circumstances of LO's death highlight that felling trees is dangerous and unpredictable," she wrote.

" Only those that possess specific training and expertise in the skill of tree felling ought to undertake the task. "

It comes almost a decade after a raft of coronial recommendations were made towards training and accreditation of private chainsaw users, none of which have been implemented.

Tree fell 'unpredictably'

On November 23, 2023, LO visited a rural property in northern Tasmania's Great Western Tiers region.

The property operated as a Buddhist monastery, which LO sometimes visited for meditation.

But on this day, he was there to cut down an 18-metre black wattle tree that was "large and twisted".

The coroner found LO was usually a "cautious and meticulous planner" with "significant experience" operating a chainsaw on his own property at Gunns Plains, about 140km north-west of Launceston.

"He was wearing a hard hat, and safety googles as he felled the tree," she wrote.

The coroner found that, as the tree fell, he "attempted to move out of its way".

"He failed to clear the tree and the head of it fell on his back, crushing him," she wrote.

When the owner of the property returned, she found LO crushed underneath the tree and contacted emergency services.

The coroner deemed the 63-year-old's death an accident.

"The weather and environmental conditions in which he was working did not contribute to the accident," she wrote.

"I find that the tree fell on LO because it had fallen unpredictably either as to the timing of or direction of its fall."

'Absence of training'

In her investigation, the coroner referenced recommendations made in 2017 following the deaths of six men, all of whom died while privately felling trees.

"One of the factors Coroner Cooper identified as common to the deaths he investigated was the absence of training," Magistrate Mackey wrote.

"Coroner Cooper made recommendations directed toward the training and accreditation of private operators of chainsaws.

" None of the recommendations have been adopted in the nine years since they were made. "

Magistrate Mackey recommended the Tasmanian government "investigate and implement regulating private tree felling activities", particularly with regard to training.

She also recommended increasing public awareness of the dangers of tree felling "by those who lack specialised training".

The state government has been contacted for comment.

title: Diarrhoea parasite spreads across US as more than 10,000 cases recorded
text:
A parasitic infection that causes diarrhoea has now reportedly spread across more than a dozen states in the US after officials blamed contaminated lettuce for the outbreak.

Taco Bell lettuce identified as one source of US 'explosive' diarrhoea outbreak A record number of cyclospora cases have been reported in more than 30 US states, but experts say not every illness is likely to have been caused by a single source.

The Cyclospora parasite causes diarrhoea, nausea, and sometimes vomiting; without treatment, symptoms can last for more than a month.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has officially linked the outbreak to nine states.

Local media, including The Washington Post, have predicted this number will soon increase to at least 15 states.

At least two deaths have also been reported in Michigan, the first fatalities associated with the outbreak.

What is Cyclospora?

Cyclosporiasis is an intestinal infection that can be contracted by consuming raw fruit and vegetables or water contaminated with the cyclospora parasite.

The microscopic parasite is transmitted via faecal matter.

It is also notoriously difficult to detect, according to professor Shokoofeh Shamsi, a parasitologist at Charles Sturt University.

"It's very easy for it to just penetrate through different aspects of our lives and infect us," she said.

Though the infection is rarely life-threatening, children, older people and immunocompromised people are at risk of serious illness stemming from it.

Loading...

Both people who died earlier this week, according to Michigan health officials, had underlying health conditions that may have been impacted by dehydration and the infection.

"Any time we get complacent, an outbreak is going to happen," Professor Shamsi said.

"Now the US, a leader in global health, is just really unable to control this outbreak.

" The two deaths [are] definitely the tip of the iceberg. Whatever you see, there is more beneath the surface. "

How did this Cyclospora outbreak start?

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has linked the outbreak to iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico.

The lettuce, supplied by Taylor Farms de Mexico, was served at Taco Bell locations in multiple states.

Taylor Farms has since announced a recall for the lettuce products sourced from Mexico, distributed to 27 states between June 29 and July 16.

The same supplier was linked to a 2013 Cyclospora outbreak, which spread across multiple states and infected hundreds of people.

An investigation into reported cases and contaminated products is ongoing by the FDA and the CDC, which said they expected to see the number of confirmed cases rise despite the product recall.

Former FDA commissioner Scott Gottlieb said weather conditions had raised the risk of contamination.

Raw sewage could have reached farmed areas through flooding or a breach, he added.

"There was some event that happened in central Mexico, we don't know what yet," he told CNBC.

" That led to a lot of fields probably getting contaminated. "

Analysts in Mexico said they were waiting for the results of official investigations. Mexico has only recorded a handful of cases since the infection began to spread.

While the majority have been linked to Taylor Farms, at least two other outbreaks under investigation have an unknown source.

Democratic congressman Josh Gottheimer blamed cuts to the FDA and CDC during the second Trump administration for the lack of surveillance.

Mr Gottheimer said the CDC had fired more than 70 per cent of the team responsible for tracking Cyclospora and other parasites since 2025.

How many cases of cyclosporiasis have been recorded so far?

As of August 3, the CDC had received reports of 10,468 cases of confirmed cyclosporiasis.

An additional 12,255 cases are still unconfirmed, and health officials have indicated these numbers likely represent only a fraction of the total outbreak.

To date 47 states have reported cases and at least 517 people have been hospitalised.

Dr Gottlieb has told media he believed cases were being under-reported.

The true number, he said, was likely 10 to 20 times what had been recorded.

"This is the largest outbreak we've ever seen in the history of Cyclospora," he said.

In Michigan, the state at the centre of the outbreak, officials have recorded 11,508 total cases, well above the CDC's total confirmed caseload.

The CDC does not include probable cases, meaning the numbers vary depending on whether state officials are combining probable and confirmed cyclosporiasis.

Michigan's chief medical executive, Natasha Bagdasarian, said local health departments were interviewing patients about what they ate and where it came from.

The information was being entered into a statewide database.

"There's a lot of tracing back that we have to do," Dr Bagdasarian said.

"[It's] not just in terms of where people got their produce from, but then tracing that back to its very origins and finding where along the pathway the contamination occurred."

How do you control the spread of Cyclospora?

For a single-celled organism, according to Professor Shamsi, cyclospora is "really difficult to kill".

"The only thing we know that is 100 per cent effective is high temperature and proper cooking," she said.

Preventing cyclosporiasis: Wash hands with soap and water before/after handling raw fruit and vegetables

Wash all produce before eating, cutting or cooking

Cook produce to at least 70 degrees Celsius

"But we don't want to cook our salads … and it's highly recommended by health professionals as well to consume salads and raw vegetables on a daily basis.

"It's not only on the public to be aware … but largely it's on policymakers and everyone in the food safety sector to have a very well designed supply system that is based on prevention.

"And if [the parasite] does make it through, they need proper surveillance and monitoring to remove those products from the food system."

There have been no outbreaks of cyclosporiasis in Australia to date, according to the Australian Drinking Water Guidelines.

Sporadic cases have been associated with international travel.

title: The ups and downs of facing housing insecurity later in life
text:
For more than a decade, finding a safe and affordable home has felt like a game of snakes and ladders for Meredith.

Securing her first social housing unit in her 50s felt like a major step up.

She stayed for three years, but living in a noisy environment, where drugs were sometimes visibly present, took its toll.

"I realised, even though I would have been beautifully housed for the rest of my life, I couldn't stay there," she said.

The search began for a new home, and she landed a winner — an affordable unit in a retirement village on the Sunshine Coast.

"I thought I was home and hosed," she said.

Calls to replace affordable housing scheme Advocates call for a National Rental Affordability Scheme 2.0 after thousands of people participating in subsidies face rent hikes.

Six years later, the federal government's rental scheme ended, and Meredith could no longer afford her unit.

She slid back to square one.

To improve her chances of finding another home, she moved back to Brisbane.

While she now has a great place to live, she knows how quickly things can change.

"There is an element of insecurity and that scares the living daylights out of me because I have already lost two fantastic housing places," she said.

" I have never been on the streets, but the insecurity has been quite severe at times because there is no backup. "

According to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 31,700 people aged 55 years and over received assistance from specialist homelessness services in 2024-25, 2,200 more than the previous year.

Of those, 54 per cent, almost 17,000, were women.

The availability of rentals in Brisbane's private market remains stubbornly tight at 1 per cent, according to the Real Estate Institute of Queensland.

The median cost of rent sits at about $700 per week.

Knowledge is power

Meredith, now in her 70s, chose not to marry and has never inherited any property. She doesn't have a car or friends with a spare room to call on.

But she is determined to keep a roof over her head.

In her bid to arm herself with information, she discovered the Housing Older Women's Support Service.

The Queensland government-funded program is dedicated to helping women over 50, and First Nations women over 45, navigate the system and move towards finding permanent housing.

What do you want to tell us? Have Your Say Our best stories start with listening to yours. Tell us what Australia should know.

For Meredith, such knowledge is power and connecting with other women has been a bonus.

"I feel like a different person knowing that if worse comes to worst and I do lose my housing, I've got all these people to turn to," she said.

The free service was established in 2022 after a group of women rallied together to call on the government to step up.

Maggie Shambrook, a founding member of the Housing Older Women Movement, said she was relieved the service was helping women like Meredith.

Maggie Shambrook is a founding participant of the Housing Older Women Movement. (ABC News: Claudia Williams)

" We're just another group in the housing crisis pool that's trying to swim, and we're drowning sadly. "

The Queensland-based service is modelled on Home at Last in Victoria, run by Housing for the Age Action Group.

It is run by Footprints Community, a not-for-profit that offers a range of support for people covering aged care, mental health, homelessness and social isolation.

Two steps forward, one step back

Women who have lent on the Housing Older Women's Support Service have shared the ups and downs they have faced through poetry, photographs and art as part of an evaluation of the service by the Queensland University of Technology.

Their experiences inspired researchers to develop a board game based on the concept of snakes and ladders.

The Queensland University of Technology design lab developed a game of snakes and ladders to raise awareness of the challenges women experiencing housing insecurity face. (ABC News: Claudia Williams)

Get financial assistance to cover bond and rent arrears? Move forward six spaces. Feeling unsafe in emergency accommodation? Back you go.

Design psychology professor Evonne Miller said the idea was to use creativity to educate and inspire empathy.

"We don't realise how we are one misfortune away from this being our story," she said. "We can do better, we need to do better to support older women who are in this precarious situation."

Queensland University of Technology design professor Evonne Miller. (ABC News: Claudia Williams)

During coffee catch-ups and workshops, Professor Miller said she was struck by the resilience the women showed and the support they gave each other.

"They are putting their lipstick on, putting their makeup on and doing their best," she said.

" They have got this public face of not wanting to share that because there is a lot of shame and fear and worry. "

For Ms Shambrook and the Housing Older Women Movement, the focus is now on pushing for a more community-led response to housing with input from those being housed.

"We don't want to be living in shoeboxes with neighbours who don't know how to be neighbours, so we need to influence that change," she said.

"We need some oomph, we need some pressure, and we need visibility because we have got lost in the housing crisis."

title: How Australia can harness home support in lead up to Brisbane 2032
text:
Water Polo Australia has hailed the enormous success of the World Cup finals in Sydney, saying that it proves Australia is in an ideal position to host more World Aquatics events in the lead up to the 2032 Brisbane Olympic Games.

Sydney hosted the eight-team World Cup finals over five days at the Sydney Olympic Park Aquatic Centre, the first time a major global Water Polo event had been hosted in the city since the 2000 Olympics.

Australia's Stingers won a hugely impressive bronze medal, following on from their memorable silver medal at the Paris Olympics to firmly establish themselves as one of Australia's most likeable and backable teams.

Meanwhile, the Sharks finished an enormously credible fourth, beating world champions Spain in a heroic penalty shoot out in the quarterfinals to underline their status as a team that is building to be a genuine medal contender for the 2032 Games.

But more importantly, more than 10,000 spectators came through the doors across the five days, creating a memorable atmosphere at the former Olympic venue.

The Stingers won a brilliant bronze medal in Sydney. (Supplied: World Aquatics/Julius Dimataga)

And the Australian players certainly appreciated it.

"To have a whole pool full of our friends and family, and the water polo community, it's really special … this is such a huge part of our careers and something that we'll never forget," Sienna Hearn said after the semifinal loss to the USA.

"The atmosphere [in Sydney] is so special for all of us and makes us want to try even harder for our friends and family."

The 'precious' bond driving the Stingers to success Australia's women's water polo team, the Stingers, were the most successful Australian team at the Paris Olympics, winning a stunning silver medal. This is the secret to their success.

Bronte Halligan noted that it was the home support that made the difference for the Stingers as they fought back from defeat against the USA to win bronze.

"Any game on home soil is unreal. But then to win a medal, at a world event, on home soil is just phenomenal," she said.

"The crowd was epic, they got us through the game, we stayed in it, we got the result and I couldn't be prouder of the girls."

Head coach Bec Rippon agreed, calling the crowd "amazing".

"We don't get many opportunities to play in these big moments — and for this team the semifinal the other day was only the second ever semifinal that we've played in," she said.

"So to have opportunities like this, under pressure, with a crowd, you can't buy that kind of experience.

"We have such a privilege of going overseas and playing in front of other nations' home crowds, so it was really amazing to be able to do that for our fans, friends and family here tonight who follow us all over the world."

Water Polo Australia hungry for more

Teenager Bless Daly is among the new guard of Australian water polo players on the rise. (Getty Images: Corbis/Steve Christo)

It's not a surprise that Water Polo Australia wants to see more of that support over the next six years and beyond.

"We were really keen to make sure we leveraged the home crowd advantage," Water Polo Australia chief executive Tim Welsford told ABC Sport the day after the tournament, his voice still hoarse from cheering on during a thrilling week of water polo.

"In the early stages of planning there was a very clear line of sight on what we wanted, to have the opportunity for kids to come into the centre, to buy a Sharks or Stingers top, to put the war paint on their face, the zinc, and sit in the crowd and support their team.

"That was a very clear vision for us about what we wanted to deliver in terms of the user experience inside the venue, and I think we went very close to nailing that.

"I think anyone who was in the venue, and it probably came across on the broadcast, will tell you how electric the atmosphere was.

"And that wasn't just the Australian games, even the men's gold medal game between Hungary and Greece, we had this beautiful picture of all the Greece fans in the blue seats, all the Hungary fans in the green seats, and we had all the Aussie water polo purists sitting in the middle.

"And at 7 o'clock on Sunday night, we still had the most incredible atmosphere."

Supporters cheer on Team Australia at the bronze medal match between Australia and Russia during the 2026 World Aquatics Water Polo World Cup at Sydney Olympic Park Aquatic Centre. (Getty Images: Andy Cheung)

Remarkably, Water Polo Australia was able to garner such incredible community buy-in with just eight months lead-in time.

Welsford said that if they were given longer, they could layer even more onto the event and what they could achieve.

"We've got an appetite to do more of this into the future," Welsford said.

"That's why we really sort of pushed to make every post a winner this time so that World Aquatics, considers us … a really safe pair of hands for them to be able to allocate events to, that they know they're going to get a great result here.

"I'm confident they walked away with that exact feeling.

"We talked often about what does success look like [for this event], and you've got all those [attendance and social media] metrics and I think that's a really important piece and we will measure those, of course.

"But the community-building success was just incredible — people that are reaching out saying, we need to host more of these.

"Australia is cherry ripe for this type of thing … There is a real appetite here for us to do this again. And so we want to support that community groundswell.

"We would love to have it back."

Bec Rippon led the Stingers to two major global medals in the last three years. (Getty Images: Corbis/Steve Christo )

Some of the metrics truly have been encouraging, with almost 14 million social media views in the lead up to and during the event, coupled with the huge attendances.

"Our numbers in the last three months have been bigger than our Olympic year in terms of the social media views," Welsford said.

"This is an unbelievable opportunity for us to be able to showcase the sport."

Water Polo, although a relatively niche sport in Australia, is huge in Europe.

And despite being a long way from the sport's heartland, one of the key features of the tournament was how much support other nations received — none of which was by accident.

Water Polo Australia reached out to the embassies of all nations participating in the event to help drum up support within their communities, which was realised in a vibrant, multicultural crowd celebrating the sport throughout the five days.

Even the thorny issue of Russia's involvement — the women's team qualified and became the first international Russian team to compete on Australian soil since the country was banned in the wake of the Ukraine War.

"I think everybody understandably was a little bit on edge a little bit around how that would play out, and we are continually empathetic to the Ukrainian community and what's going on over there at the moment," Welsford said, noting that Australia, as an organising committee, does not get the option to select which teams qualify for the event.

"So it's our job to then accept our lot and make the best of the situation and try and put on a great show for everyone," he added.

"We did have a Ukrainian protest, they were really well organised, extremely peaceful, they did everything they could to amplify their message and we thank them for doing it in the way that they did as well."

National Aquatic Centre essential for aquatics legacy

Australia will hope for even more events in the lead up to 2032 as the dream of a National Aquatic Centre is realised. (Getty Images: Andy Cheung)

A key factor in being able to host more events will be the development of the National Aquatic Centre in Brisbane, a venue that Water Polo Australia, along with their diving and artistic swimming counterparts, really lobbied for before getting Swimming Australia on board.

"The National Aquatic Centre concept was actually initiated firstly by water polo, but then in conjunction with diving and artistic swimming," Welsford said.

"Under Rob Woodhouse's leadership, [Swimming Australia] sort of joined the scheme a couple of years ago, but it was largely driven by the other three aquatic sports.

Proposed design for 2032 aquatic centre revealed The state has chosen three firms to design the aquatic centre: ARM Architecture, NH Architecture and Queensland-based Arkhefield.

"But since Rob's come on board, it's been fantastic that it's been all four of us and we've been really well united and supportive of each other, making sure that we can all get something that's really ticks the legacy box for us.

"People will talk about 2032 and what that means, but even last night talking to the Sydney 2000 crew, there were so many events in the lead into 2000 that we hosted here locally.

"People and countries wanted to come out and have that experience prior [to the Games].

"So in the context of us hosting this year, this is the start of it for us.

"We want more of these international style events here over the next six years and we believe countries will want to come, particularly given the experience they've had over the last five or six days.

"We want to do more of that as we move forward.

"The National Aquatic Centre delivers us that legacy venue that we need. I think if anybody experienced what Sydney Olympic Park was able to do for us — not that was built for the Olympics, but it was the Olympic venue — it stands up so well in terms of a legacy asset for us to be able to use.

"You know, 26 years after the Olympic Games and 30 years after it's been built, it's still being used as a world-class event for aquatics.

"It's a phenomenal opportunity that we need to make sure we get right in terms of the National Aquatic Centre."

title: 'Shocking': Hospital inquiry urges axing of public-private partnership
text:
"Shocking revelations" have led to a NSW parliamentary inquiry calling for a Newcastle hospital to be put back in public hands.

The Calvary Mater Hospital, which operates under a public-private partnership, is one of the leading cancer hospitals in regional NSW, with some patients travelling hours to receive care.

But it has been under intense scrutiny over the past 12 months, after a mould infestation was found in the hospital's cancer unit, and maggots were found spread across the hospital floor.

The parliamentary inquiry was chaired by Greens MP Dr Amanda Cohn, who said in a statement the revelations shared by staff and whistleblowers were "shocking".

"We heard about maggots falling from the ceiling onto a patient, nurses funnelling rainwater into garbage bins during the night, a doctor fainting during surgery because of high humidity in the operating theatre, and explosive allegations of falsified maintenance records," she said.

"All these problems could have been prevented.

" Hospital management and the NSW government knew about these issues for years, and failed to address them. "

The report recommends the NSW Government terminate the current public-private partnership and bring ownership and management of the hospital directly into NSW Health as soon as reasonably possible. .

It also recommends the Orange and Bathurst Hospital public-private partnerships be analysed for value, including whether services should be returned to direct public management by the Western NSW Local Health District.

The committee heard explosive allegations from staff across three public hearings. (ABC Newcastle: Nakita Jager)

Speaking in the Hunter region late last month, Premier Chris Minns said the public-private contract was a costly mistake, but not one that could be easily undone.

"We're committed to making the situation far better at the Mater," he said.

"We don't want that privatised model of care

" [But] we have to examine the scope of that deal so that taxpayers don't have to foot the bill. "

Following the mould discovery, the state government commenced rectification works on the building, including the replacement of non-compliant cladding.

Union welcomes findings

In a statement, Health Services Union Secretary Gerard Hayes said the recommendations made by the committee must be implemented urgently.

"Our members at the Calvary Mater have been raising the alarm about mould, potable water failures, intimidation of whistleblowers and a 'sweep it under the rug' culture for close to a decade," he said.

"The committee has listened, and the recommendation that the hospital return to public hands is a moment of accountability.

Mr Hayes said the findings showed a "clear message about the failure of the public-private partnership model in our health system".

"Whether it's the Northern Beaches or Newcastle, staff and patients are put at risk," he said.

"It's time to end the failed experiment."

The ABC has approached the Calvary Care and NSW Health for comment.

title: Stokes claims cricket has drinking culture, not just England
text:
Former England captain Ben Stokes has hit back at claims his side had a drinking problem, instead claiming cricket as a sport has a drinking culture.

Stokes, who abruptly retired in June, appeared on a podcast with former England teammate Stuart Broad where he addressed a range of different topics.

Among those was a suggestion that England's team has a drinking problem after a number of off-field incidents during last summer's ill-fated Ashes tour to Australia.

"God, that's such an extreme thing to put on a team," Stokes told Broad on the For Love Of Cricket podcast when asked whether England had a drinking problem.

Ben Stokes's retirement a perfect example of his main character energy Ben Stokes has been the centre of England's cricketing universe for 15 years. In announcing his retirement mid-match, he highlighted how damaging that main character energy can be.

"I think cricket has just a drinking culture and it hasn't changed. We're in 2026 where the game has gone more professional over the years, and one thing that I think has just stayed within cricket is its relationship with alcohol, from club cricket and then works its way up. It's just stayed there and it's been embedded within the sport.

"The relationship with alcohol and cricket is just something that hasn't moved on as the game of cricket has become more professional.

"There's been more science and medicine, there's more nutritional information, there's more this, there's more that, but the one thing that has been a constant and stayed around and has been for a very long time is its relationship with alcohol.

"So for people who think that the English cricket team has a drinking culture, I'd say no.

" I would just say cricket has culture that is associated with alcohol. "

England's team under Stokes faced heavy criticism during its mid-Ashes break in Noosa last year, which came with the team already in an 0-2 hole.

Opener Ben Duckett was filmed by fans while heavily intoxicated and struggling to find his way back to England's hotel, while during the final Test in Sydney, it emerged that vice-captain Harry Brook had gotten into an altercation with a bouncer on the team's New Zealand tour.

"I think it can be a problem," Stokes said of cricket's drinking culture.

"If you look at everything over the years, you look at a lot of people that have been involved within cricket and have had bad relationships with alcohol. It's just, I don't know what you do to change it."

Ben Stokes's Ashes understudy Harry Brook (right) was involved in an altercation with a nightclub bouncer in New Zealand prior to the Ashes. (Getty Images: Gareth Copley/ECB)

Stokes also referenced his own personal experience with alcohol throughout his career.

He was arrested in 2017 after his involvement in a street brawl near a nightclub with then-teammate Alex Hales and served an eight-match suspension for the incident.

"I've had … I don't want to say problems, but I've had relationships with alcohol at times over my career that have been potentially dangerous, if that makes sense, but it's completely different to me now," he said.

"I just think that there's this relationship with alcohol within cricket that has been the same from the 80s.

Former Australian Test batter David Boon (centre) has become well known for his love of beer, namely the 52 he consumed on a flight to the UK. (Getty Images: PA Images)

"As the game has got better and better and better, that thing has just stayed around. That's my opinion on cricket and alcohol."

Stokes's theory regarding cricket and its athletes' relationship to alcohol is not without credence.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

In Australian cricket, the story of David Boon drinking 52 beers on a flight to the UK ahead of the 1989 Ashes series is spoken about as the stuff of legend.

Boon appeared on a podcast in 2023 saying he regretted the whole episode.

"I've got to be brutally honest here, I won't deny it happened. We all do stupid things in our lives and I'll finish by just being serious," he said on the BackChat Sports Show.

"You have fun, you do something and then you think: 'Shit, what about the ramifications to everything else', to your family, to your children.

""It caused some crap over the years, and it's something that I regret a lot. Can't deny it but I do regret it. And I was stupid to be able to do that when you're in the public eye."

title: Gas giant prosecuted after under-reporting toxic emissions
text:
The Northern Territory's environmental regulator has charged Japanese gas giant Inpex for under-reporting the amount of toxic emissions it released from the Ichthys facility near Darwin.

The NT Environment Protection Authority (EPA) said it decided to prosecute after Inpex told the regulator it had significantly under-reported the level of benzene and toluene emissions between 2019 and 2024.

In a statement, the NT EPA said the under-reporting allegedly represented a breach of Inpex's environmental licence to operate.

"The NT EPA licences Ichthys LNG through an environment protection licence, originally granted on 13 December 2017," the statement said.

"Under the licence, Ichthys LNG is required to annually report total emissions to air in tonnes to the NT EPA.

"In October 2025, Ichthys LNG informed the NT EPA of significant under-reporting of emissions from the Ichthys LNG facility. The NT EPA has now commenced prosecution in relation to this matter."

The NT EPA recently recommended changes to the licences of Darwin's two major gas processing companies, Santos and Inpex, after Inpex's under-reporting triggered a review.

The NT EPA said it would not provide further comment while the matter is before the courts.

It is understood the matter will appear in Darwin Local Court, but a date is yet to be finalised.

Inpex was contacted for comment.

More to come.

title: High Court rules in favour of native title holders fighting NT water licence
text:
Native title holders from Central Australia have won their fight to assert cultural rights over an aquifer located on their lands.

The High Court of Australia today decided in favour of the Mpwerempwer Aboriginal Corporation (MAC), which had challenged a plan to turn thousands of hectares on Singleton Station, south of Tennant Creek, into an irrigated horticulture business.

The station's lessees, Fortune Agribusiness, plan to grow mandarins, table grapes, avocados, muskmelons, and other fruits.

The endeavour would transform the cattle property into one of the nation's biggest fruit farms, requiring 40,000 megalitres (40 billion litres) of water every year once fully developed.

That demand was at the heart of the appeal brought by MAC, which submitted that water was only available from an underground aquifer accessed by bores on the property.

It claimed water, and sites traditionally associated with access to or use of water, have significance for traditional occupants of arid lands.

The traditional owners say they are concerned the licence will lead to the destruction of too many sacred water sites. (Supplied: Anna Miers, Central Land Council)

Claim water licence had not been lawfully granted

The 2020 application by Fortune for the 30-year water licence was described by the Department of Environment at the time as being "possibly the largest volume application in a single water resource by a single entity in Australia".

Lawyers for MAC claimed the water licence had not been lawfully granted because the minister in charge did not properly justify granting the water licence for 30 years rather than the standard 10-year period.

They also argued Aboriginal cultural values had not been considered in the making of that decision, and that native title holders had been denied procedural fairness by decision makers.

The NT government said in its submissions the law did not require the decision-maker to consider the impact on Aboriginal cultural values. (ABC Alice Springs: Samantha Jonscher)

MAC, which is made up of traditional owners and native title holders from four Aboriginal landholding groups, had failed in their bid to overturn the licence in challenges heard by the Northern Territory Supreme Court and Court of Appeal over the last four years.

The native title and traditional owners said they were concerned the licence would lead to the destruction of too many sacred water sites and affect native plants and animals that depend on the water.

In February, traditional owner Valerie Ngapangardi Curtis said the licence would be damaging in multiple ways.

"If they take too much water, it's going to damage our country, it's going to damage all our plants and animals, and it's going to damage our culture as well and dreaming and storyline," she said.

Minister denied MAC procedural fairness, court finds

For its part, the Northern Territory government and Fortune had argued the minister responsible was not legally obliged to consider special circumstances, including any cultural values impact assessment.

But today, the High Court unanimously agreed the water licence had not been lawfully granted by the Northern Territory government.

It found the minister had not properly satisfied circumstances that justified the extended 30-year licence, and that the minister had denied MAC procedural fairness in not providing a reasonable opportunity to make its case about conditions imposed on the licence.

The High Court ruled in favour of traditional owners. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The decision means the water licence will be quashed and the process referred back to the minister responsible, who will also have to consider the territory's environmental approvals processes associated with the site.

Fortune must also pay the costs of MAC's appeal, but limited only to those that went towards its arguments about procedural fairness, with the Supreme Court to determine other costs.

Fortune Agribusiness reviewing judgement with legal team

In a statement, Fortune Agribusiness said it noted the High Court decision and was reviewing the judgement and its implications with its legal team.

"We respect the Court's decision and will carefully consider the reasons for the judgment before making any further comment," a company spokesperson said.

"Singleton Farm remains an important long-term development opportunity for Central Australia, with the potential to deliver substantial benefits to many stakeholders.

"Fortune Agribusiness maintains its long-standing commitment to constructive engagement with native title holders and the Central Land Council and will continue to seek an agreed pathway to deliver these benefits in a respectful and collaborative manner."

title: Hobart wharf demolition paving way for new icebreaker berth
text:
A "complex" operation to deconstruct an aging wharf in Hobart has begun, paving the way for a new home berth for Australia's Antarctic icebreaker, RSV Nuyina.

The Macquarie Wharf 6 demolition is part of a broader wharf redevelopment project aimed at modernising Tasmania's port network and providing a marine base for Australia's Antarctic program.

TasPorts CEO Allan Gray said more than 12,900 tonnes of concrete, steel and timber would be "carefully separated, broken down and removed".

"Deconstructing a structure of this size over water is a genuinely complex undertaking," Captain Gray said.

The demolition works are expected to take five months. (Supplied: www.robburnettimages.com)

Specialised marine equipment will be used, from a 280-tonne crawler crane to excavators fitted with rock breakers, shears and pulverisers.

"With works taking place on the River Derwent, environmental controls, including protective silt curtains and marine-life monitoring, are in place to protect the local environment throughout the works," Captain Gray said.

The wharf, which was riddled with concrete cancer, will be demolished in sections, followed by construction and piling for the new wharf.

The project received $188 million from the federal government.

Surrounding wharves will also be upgraded. (Supplied: www.robburnettimages.com)

Federal Member for Franklin Julie Collins said it was "terrific" to see the project underway.

" Hobart is a crucial hub for Antarctic and Southern Ocean science in Australia. We're proud to be investing in Tasmania to ensure it remains our gateway to Antarctica for years to come. "

Wharves 4 and 5 will also be upgraded as part of the wider works.

The project is being touted as good for employment and delivery of goods. (Supplied: www.robburnettimages.com)

Tasmania's Infrastructure and Transport Minister, Kerry Vincent, said the renewal of assets was important.

"This will have ongoing great effects for Hobart and the surrounding areas, not just employment but supply of goods as well, and it gives upgraded facilities for TasPorts," Mr Vincent said.

" In years to come, [this will] give better facilities and stronger berthing for the bigger ships, the larger cruise ships that are being built all around the world, and for cargo ships to come in. "

Nuyina's refuelling saga ongoing

The redevelopment of the wharf into the new home berth for RSV Nuyina is due for completion in 2028.

But the state and federal governments are yet to agree on a solution for Nuyina's expensive and lengthy refuelling journey to Burnie in the state's north-west.

The icebreaker must travel 674 kilometres, costing almost $900,000 extra each year, because it is unable to refuel at Selfs Point, a few kilometres from its Macquarie Wharf home port.

This is due to a ban on the ship travelling under the Tasman Bridge, after TasPorts' harbourmaster determined Nuyina lacked the "directional stability" required for a safe transit under the bridge.

In 1975, the Tasman Bridge partially collapsed after an ore carrier struck the pylons, causing the deaths of 12 people.

Infrastructure Minister Kerry Vincent says a refuelling solution is close. (ABC News: Owain Stia James)

The state government promised in 2024 to find a refuelling solution as part of the Macquarie Wharf upgrade deal with the Commonwealth.

Speaking today, Minister Vincent said discussions were in the final stages.

title: Growers find expanding markets to save bumper avocado crop from oversupply
text:
The avocado industry is experiencing another high-volume crop year, but unlike previous years with oversupply, the fruit is finding a market.

Increasing domestic consumption and record export volumes have helped absorb the bumper harvest, a stark turnaround from just a few seasons ago when the market struggled to cope with high production.

The Avocado Collective, which markets and supports avocado growers across Australia, said the industry was strategic in selling this year's crop.

The group's Brent Chambers said during the opening weeks of Queensland's Shepard avocado season, which typically ran from February to April, almost the entire crop was exported.

"We see there's great value in exporting Shepards early, removing them from the domestic market to ensure that growers get the best economic return," he said.

Brent Chambers says the industry is sending more early fruit out for export. (ABC Rural: Sophie Johnson)

Far North Queensland grower and Avocados Australia director Lawrence Massasso said rising domestic consumption had improved the industry's ability to handle large crops.

"During the Shepard season we had supply up around 600 to 650,000 trays a week, which two or three seasons ago we would have said that was impossible to clear [but] that fruit cleared every week," he said.

"We have more and more really committed [Australian] customers who will continue to support us come hell or high water."

The volume of fruit coming to market has resulted in lower prices, with Shepard avocados retailing for as low as 90 cents per piece.

"We weren't [making good money]. But the fruit was clearing and growers were getting a return on that crop," Mr Massasso said.

Lawrence Massasso says domestic consumption has increased significantly in the past few years. (ABC Rural: Sophie Johnson)

Export numbers

Rabobank senior analyst Michael Harvey said national production could reach about 170,000 metric tonnes in coming seasons, with Queensland continuing to produce about half of Australia's crop.

"Queensland's still the largest producing state … we're still heading towards a record production in the coming years and that will mean greater exports as well," he said.

Up to 30 per cent of the national crop was exported this season, with record numbers sent overseas.

Hong Kong, Singapore and Malaysia remain key markets, while Japan and Thailand continue to emerge.

By the end of June, Australian avocado exports were more than 50 per cent higher than the same time last year.

Mr Harvey said global demand was keeping pace with rising production.

"Global avocado exports are continuing to grow at a rapid rate. In fact, in the last 15 years, you've seen a fourfold expansion in global exports of avocado," Mr Harvey said.

"Global avocado consumption is growing, there is obviously increasing production to meet that growing demand."

Rabobank says national production of avocados could reach about 170,000 metric tonnes. (ABC Rural: Sophie Johnson)

Smaller crop in 2027

Western Australia is the country's second largest producing state.

Mr Chambers said this year it produced about 13.5 million trays of avocados, but next year, that number was expected to drop significantly to 5 million trays.

It was due to behaviour cycles in the crop, where after a strong yielding year, the trees typically produced less fruit.

Mr Chambers said the smaller crop was likely to lift supermarket prices nationally, particularly during summer.

"[Prices] are going to be pretty buoyant during that January, February period," he said.

However, he expected production to rebound in 2028 as Western Australia and north Queensland returned with strong crops.

"Again, the strategy will be how much can we move offshore," he said.

"If we start developing those relationships now, hopefully we can keep that price relatively high."

title: Age is just a number as Roar announce youngest-ever A-League manager
text:
Brisbane Roar have made A-League history, announcing the youngest-ever manager to lead the women's side moving forward.

At just 27 years of age, Johnathan Clemente has been named the new Roar coach ahead of the ALW season.

He arrives at Brisbane on a two-year deal, coming from Melbourne Victory where he was an assistant under Jeff Hopkins with the ALW side.

"I am incredibly honoured at the opportunity to lead one of the most successful clubs in the country, with one of the best squads in the league and to do it in one of the most beautiful places in the world," Clemente said in a statement.

"I see exciting parallels between Brisbane Roar and my own journey. We've been hungry, ambitious and have spent the past few years building strong foundations. Now it's our time to come together and establish ourselves at the pinnacle of women's football in this country."

Despite his young age, Clemente has plenty of coaching and managerial experience.

He was the youngest ever head coach of a National Premier League side when he took over Heidelberg United at the age of 20.

During his three seasons with the club, 10 players were developed and signed to A-League squads.

During his time with Victory, Clemente also led the NPLW, Female Pathways and the Melbourne Victory Afghan Women's Team programs.

Brisbane Roar finished fourth on the ALW table last season, and lost their two-leg semifinal to Wellington Phoenix 3-2 on aggregate, going to extra time in the second leg.

"Alex Smith and the squad were tremendous last season, finishing fourth and were one game away from a grand final, with a host of exciting, young, local talent. "I'll be looking to build on the great work, create consistency and continue the upward trajectory of the program," Clemente said.

"Our team will be built around shared principles, not set structures, with the objective being not how we play, but how we feel.

"We want our fans to believe in the fluid football they'll see, we want our young girls in the crowd to believe they can represent Brisbane one day and we want our squad to believe that when you represent our team and our state, anything is possible."

Women in Sport Spotlight We put the spotlight on women making a big impact on and off the field in the sporting world — from the grassroots through to the elite level.

The previous youngest managers were both 29 years of age, when Jess Fishlock took charge of Melbourne City in the W-League during the 2016-17 season, and Alex Epakis when he became manager of Perth Glory ALW side in 2020.

The youngest manager of an ALM side was Des Buckingham, who was 31 when he became manager of Wellington in 2017.

The Roar are not worried about Clemente's age, with sporting director James Gow stating the 27-year-old impressed when the club was recruiting for a new manager.

"Johnathan is a coach with a very clear idea of how he wants to play, train and develop his team. We conducted a thorough recruitment process, and his desire for the role and clarity in how he works stood out," Gow said.

"Despite his young age, he has a lot of experience in the A-League Women's space. He really buys into the strategy we as a club wish to execute. We are looking forward to welcoming him and seeing him get to work."

The ALW and ALM seasons will both begin in mid-October.

title: Blistering Marsh knock helps Sunrisers smash Hundred's record score
text:
A brutal assault by Mitch Marsh has proved the launch pad for a record total by Leeds Sunrisers in The Hundred competition at Headingley.

The West Australian battered 76 off 37 balls with seven sixes to send the franchise on its way to 2-241 off 100 balls, the highest score in the competition's six years, 15 runs better than the previous record.

Opponents London Spirit were never in the hunt on Tuesday (Wednesday AEST), despite finishing with 6-204 themselves.

Marsh and Ryan Rickelton broke the record for the highest partnership for any wicket in the competition, 148 from 65 balls.

"I'm very routine on game day, trying to stay relaxed, which I am not, but once I get started I try and get into the game and build partnerships," said Marsh.

"Partnerships are very important to us."

The 34-year-old, who now has 290 runs in five innings for Sunrisers with a lowest score of 41, added he loves batting at Headingley, where he also made a run-a-ball Ashes century in 2023.

The carnage continued after Marsh's dismissal with South African Rickelton slamming an unbeaten 94 off 42 balls and local hero Harry Brook carving 55 off 18 deliveries with some astonishing shots.

Adam Zampa (pictured) copped the brunt of the punishment from his Australian teammate Marsh. (Getty Images: Phillip Brown)

Among the mauled bowlers was Aussie leg-spinner Adam Zampa, whose 10 deliveries went for 33 with one dot ball and four sixes.

His first set of five balls, to Marsh, went for 25: six, four, six, wide, six, dot, with the last ball following a strategic time-out mid-set.

Zampa's second set came immediately after Marsh's dismissal, caught at deep cover miscuing a drive.

Andrew Tye's 20 balls went for a relatively creditable 42.

"Hell of a lot of fun," said Brook.

"I thought the way Mitch Marsh and Ryan Rickelton started was incredible. Not seen anyone hit the ball as hard as Marsh.

"Marsh loves batting here. Rickelton got more runs, but he really set the tone in those first 50 balls," said former England bowler Stuart Broad on commentary.

London Spirit never got going in response, losing Yorkshire favourite Jonny Bairstow for a second-ball duck and slumping to 5-56.

Nathan Ellis dismissed the danger man, Liam Livingstone, for an 11-ball 34, and took 2-42 in his 20.

After Donald Brevis went for 38 off 21 balls, David Willey, with 83 not out off 46 balls, helped Spirit rescue their net run-rate, but the destination of the night's points had long been decided.

title: Erectile dysfunction drug may heighten risk of eye disease, study shows
text:
Men who use a Viagra-like erectile dysfunction drug long-term are "significantly more likely" to develop glaucoma than those who do not, according to a new study.

The research, published in the British Journal of Ophthalmology, followed 74,000 men aged 40 years and older, half of whom had been prescribed tadalafil (sold under the brand names such as Cialis) over a period of five years.

Along with its use to treat erectile dysfunction, the drug is also used for the long-term treatment of urinary tract problems such as increased urgency associated with an enlarged prostate.

The researchers found people who used the drug long-term were 22 per cent more likely to develop glaucoma — a common eye disease which often leads to blindness — than those who did not.

"This is the first cohort study to show there is a correlation between taking these medications and an increased risk of developing glaucoma," said Flora Hui, an optometrist and research fellow at the Centre for Eye Research Australia, who did not contribute to the study.

Dr Hui said while the study showed the risk of having glaucoma was "statistically higher" in those who took the drug, the overall risk was still "quite low".

But, she said, it highlighted the importance of getting eyes tested before, and during the time of taking these medications, especially if a person had glaucoma risk factors.

"If you're a bit older, especially if you have a family history of glaucoma … and if you're going to be on long-term therapy, you really need to have regular eye tests because glaucoma can be largely symptomless."

Glaucoma can lead to permanent vision loss. (Getty Images: Tetra Images)

PDE5i drugs and eye health

Tadalafil is part of a class of drugs called phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors (PDE5i), a group which also includes sildenafil (sold under the brand name Viagra).

Previous studies have linked PDE5i drugs with ophthalmological side effects, including those that affect the optic nerve, but until now, there has not been any research showing a strong link between a person taking tadalafil long-term and then developing glaucoma.

'Silent thief of sight' A headache is a common occurrence for many of us, but for Effie, it was the first sign that she had glaucoma.

PDE5i inhibitors block a protein called PDE-5, increasing blood flow to the penis and helping people develop and maintain an erection.

They also relax muscle tissue and improve blood flow in organs such as the prostate and bladder.

While scientists still do not know exactly how these drugs increased a person's risk of developing glaucoma, Dr Hui said there were a few working theories.

People had a finite amount of blood in their body, Dr Hui said, which meant it had to "pull the blood from somewhere" to encourage it to go elsewhere.

"We think that maybe it can transiently increase the eye pressure in people on these medications, or maybe it's taking blood away from the optic nerve at the back of the eye, which is what gets affected in glaucoma," Dr Hui said.

"If you're getting transient episodes where you don't get sufficient blood to the nerve, then that can increase the chance of injury to the nerve and then potentially increase your risk of developing glaucoma."

Flora Hui says the study highlighted the need for increased eye health checks. (Supplied: Centre for Eye Research Australia)

Although the study was observational and did not prove that taking tadalafil caused participants to develop glaucoma, Dr Hui said it showed a "clear correlation" between the two, and highlighted the need for more in-depth research.

Andrew White, a clinician scientist ophthalmologist at Westmead Hospital and Westmead Institute for Medical Research, who did not contribute to the study, added that not everyone who took these drugs experienced the same side effects, or had any side effects at all.

Dr White said while some people experienced a temporary increase in pressure in the eye, others experienced low blood pressure.

"One of the other things that we have known for quite a long time is that if your blood pressure is too low or your blood pressure control varies a lot, then your glaucoma can also get worse," he said.

And the more "pressure spikes" someone experienced, the more likely they were to either develop glaucoma or make it worse, Dr White said.

Study participants not 'healthy'

The study, led by researchers from Taiwan, used data from 73,854 men from an international health database called TriNetX, excluding anyone with a history of glaucoma.

Researchers matched 36,927 people who used tadalafil with 36,927 men who did not use any PDE5i drugs.

While the drug is used to treat erectile dysfunction, small doses can also be taken daily over the long term to treat urinary tract symptoms.

The study found those who were prescribed the drug for urinary tract symptoms were 22 per cent more likely to develop glaucoma; 32 per cent more likely to have ocular hypertension and 33 per cent more likely to start glaucoma treatment than those who did not take it.

"Tadalafil use for lower urinary tract symptoms was associated with a significant increase in the risk of glaucoma, ocular hypertension, primary open-angle glaucoma and initiation of glaucoma treatment in a large, multinational, real-world cohort," researchers concluded.

The study found the risk increased in men aged over 50.

Tadalafil is a type of drug known as a phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor. (Getty Images: Bloomberg)

The study itself had a number of key limitations, including that most of the participants were white, and therefore the findings may not apply to men of other ethnicities.

And they were not able to factor in changes in medication or the development of other underlying conditions, which could increase someone's risk of developing glaucoma.

And this was important, Dr Hui said, as other variables could affect someone's eye health.

"We're not looking at what we call healthy participants to start with," she said.

"About 40 per cent of them have high blood pressure, about 40 per cent of them have high cholesterol. These people do have comorbidities.

"It's a bit inconclusive about whether the additional chronic conditions made a difference."

Eye health monitoring needed

Although the study found a link between long-term use of tadalafil and glaucoma, the researchers stressed men should not stop using the drug for treatment of urinary tract symptoms.

Instead, they said, it indicated the need to have regular eye checks.

Dr Hui agreed.

"It's sometimes not the first thing we think about when we're taking these medications, but it's really important to get tested before you're starting these medications and if you are currently on them to get regular eye checks as well," she said.

Professor White said good monitoring and early intervention could improve someone's outcomes.

"If there is a reason for you to be monitored more closely, your local optometrist is a great start," he said.

"And the sooner we can pick something up, the sooner we can get on with treatment."

Dr Hui added that, for many, taking erectile dysfunction drugs could greatly improve someone's quality of life.

So a discussion about the potential risks and benefits was something for each patient to weigh up with their doctor.

title: Outback town says grid connection key to capturing AI investment
text:
As Australia races to build the infrastructure behind the AI boom, an outback Queensland mayor says the next generation of data centres should be built hundreds of kilometres from the nearest city.

Behind the rapid rise of artificial intelligence is a growing network of data centres built to keep up with the spike in demand for computing power and storage.

With about 250 data centres operating across the country, some communities have begun pushing back over their proximity to urban areas.

In the north-west Queensland town of Cloncurry, about 120 kilometres east of Mount Isa, Mayor Greg Campbell says the bush could prove the perfect home for the critical infrastructure.

"I've been talking about data centres with different companies for many years … but in the last month, I've had two return calls from companies," Cr Campbell said.

"I think these companies are trying to get ahead and looking to areas … outside that urban area."

Greg Campbell hopes a concrete timeline for CopperString can give industry certainty in the region. (Supplied: Cloncurry Shire Council)

Data centres hinge on CopperString

Data centres have traditionally required considerable water to transfer heat away from their servers and large energy loads to fuel computing power.

Efficiency gains through closed-loop systems and water recycling in new generations of data centres have reduced the amount of water required, but power remains the biggest hurdle in places like north-west Queensland.

Cloncurry, like all communities across the region, is not connected to the national energy market, relying on decentralised renewable projects and large diesel generators to power the area.

Greg Campbell says the region could be the perfect home for data centres trying to avoid pushback from urban centres. (ABC News: Meghan Dansie)

The state government has committed to connecting the region to the east coast through the CopperString project, but Cr Campbell said there was still no firm timeline for construction.

"CopperString is probably the precursor to turn that interest into a genuine business," he said.

"Because the north west isn't connected to the national electricity market, the mines, predominantly as the biggest users, will say that it's some of the dearest power probably in the world.

" We need that commitment to turn into a deliverable so that these companies can make bankable decisions. "

As demand and reliance on AI grows, perceptions around data centres have shifted. What was once seen as a commercial asset is now viewed as something of strategic importance.

The remote town of Cloncurry is about 120 kilometres east of Mount Isa. (ABC North West Qld: Meghan Dansie)

Australian Strategic Policy Institute deputy director Raelene Lockhorst believes the centres should be viewed as essential infrastructure.

"Where we build data centres is now a national security decision, not just a commercial one," Ms Lockhorst said.

"Northern Australia offers the combination that makes it the natural place to start: abundant land, renewable-energy potential, international cable connectivity, proximity to Indo-Pacific markets and rising strategic importance.

"Rather than retrofitting this infrastructure into already constrained metropolitan areas, the north lets us build Australia's next generation of digital infrastructure where it strengthens both economic development and national resilience."

Raelene Lockhorst says northern Australia's ample space and resources make it the ideal location to expand data centres. (ABC News: Michael Barnett)

Queensland Treasurer David Janetzki said proposed data centres in north-west Queensland could seek support for local energy solutions through the government's $200 million North West Energy Fund.

But the treasurer would not provide a delivery date for the western section of CopperString, saying the government's immediate focus was the eastern link between Townsville and Hughenden.

'Trillion-dollar question'

The United States Studies Centre said Australia's data centre sector had expanded considerably since 2020 and global demand for infrastructure was forecast to double by 2030.

University of Queensland economist Flavio Menezes said guessing how long the investment boom would last was the "trillion-dollar question".

"In 2023, $500 billion of the United States GDP … was data centres and the number keeps going up," Professor Menezes said.

"Data centres are like the heavy industry of this century.

"They produce the computing power that has become really the essential input for our digital economies.

"It [investment] all relies on computing power, and that demand keeps going up … there will be a natural limit for that investment but, if you think about the next two, three, four years, it will keep going up."

Flavio Menezes says understanding how long the data centre boom will last is the "trillion-dollar question". (ABC Radio Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

CopperString's western leg is managed by Queensland Investment Corporation and will rely on private capital to be completed.

Professor Menezes said demand from data centres would help strengthen the business case for CopperString, but warned people to be wary of the drawback.

Flavio Menezes says data centres should be seen as the "heavy industry" of the 21st century. (ABC News: Jerry Rickard)

"Data centres can bring a large number of benefits to the regional economy … the additional demand may make the case for CopperString make more economic sense as well," he said.

"Done well, they can support the case for that connection … but it's important to remember benefits go to the wider community.

"But there's hyperlocal costs in terms of pollution and competition for electricity.

"I wouldn't want to live by one."

title: The unknown corner of North Africa that has been seen by billions
text:

There’s something about this remote spot close to the western edge of the vast Sahara Desert that feels eerily familiar. I’m standing in a historic fortified village made entirely of rammed earth, clay, straw and wood that towers high above the dusty plains and valley below. Everywhere around me, in all directions, are crumbling networks of winding paths leading ever upwards, and one large flat arena, all brushed the same muted hue of old burnt toffee. A Berber man in front of the historic wooden gate of Ait Benhaddou. iStock I’ve never been to this part of Morocco, along the old caravan route between the Sahara and the fabled ancient market city of Marrakesh, and have never even heard anything about it. So why on earth do I have this strange sensation that I know it well? Then I spy a tiny restaurant along one of the spider web of alleyways. It’s called Gladiator. Two doors down is a souvenir stall, selling photographs from the TV drama Game of Thrones.

Advertisement

And, finally, it sinks in. This tiny 11th-century corner of North Africa with its intact 17th-century structures might be virtually unknown to most of us, but it’s been seen on screen by billions of people worldwide. That’s as the site where Maximus Decimus Meridius, played by a young Russell Crowe, fought for his life to enact vengeance on his enemies, and where Daenerys Targaryen marched up to the earthen walls with her army to free the slaves. Sign up for the Traveller Deals newsletter Get exclusive travel deals delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up now. Ait Benhaddou – the village that launched a thousand movies. iStock So, of all the gin joints, in all the towns, in all the world – to quote Humphrey Bogart in Casablanca, another classic set just 420 kilometres north of here – Ait Benhaddou in southern Morocco is one of the oldest, and best-preserved complete ksars (fortified villages) on earth, and one that could comfortably stand in for any ancient empire facing dark days. For today’s set-jetting tourists – those who love to visit the places where their favourite films were shot – this place glows head and shoulders over its cinematic rivals. The UNESCO-listed mud-brick citadel, topped with a granary from which there are magnificent 360-degree views, has inspired everyone who’s visited, and continues to inspire all those who watch the films and TV series that have been shot here.

Advertisement

And that’s all the way back to scenes in the 1962 epic Lawrence of Arabia, and all the way forward to this year’s mega-hit The Odyssey, directed by Christopher Nolan. Yes, of course. Where else could honestly look such a fitting ancient backcloth for Homer’s classic poem? Admiring the landscape around Ait Benhaddou. iStock In between, there have been some scorchers – The Man Who Would Be King, starring Sean Connery and Michael Caine in 1975; The Jewel of the Nile, with Michael Douglas, Kathleen Turner and Danny DeVito in 1985; and Martin Scorsese’s The Last Temptation of Christ in 1988. There’s The Mummy from Brendan Fraser and Rachel Weisz in 1999; Ridley Scott’s Kingdom of Heaven in 2005 with Orlando Bloom; and even Nicole Kidman got to stay for the 2015 Werner Herzog film, Queen of the Desert. But standing there, in this still-intact slice of the old world, its rugged paths worn by millions of footsteps over the centuries, its ancient walls constructed using medieval methods and designed to repel all invaders, its small homes still inhabited by several families … It’s a stunning glimpse of life from a long-ago age.

The ritual hoisting of your carry-on bag into the overhead bin on a Jetstar flight? Come February, you’re going to have to pay for the priority to put your bag there. Jetstar announced today it will reduce passengers’ free carry-on allowance to a single item, down from two, and begin charging a fee for guaranteed access to overhead bin space. Unpaid carry-on items will still be permitted in the overhead compartments, but only after the cash-paying priority travellers get first dibs. Jetstar passengers are now being forced to compete in the carry-on Hunger Games. Jetstar is changing its policy for carry-on baggage. What’s galling is that the “new product” – access to the overhead bin – was formerly a standard product. Jetstar’s marketing is a sleight of hand, of sorts. As consumer advocate Adam Glezer notes: “You’re not paying for a bin. You’re paying for a better chance at one.”

Related Article Aviation New consumer protections would undermine Jetstar’s ‘existence’: CEO It’s the same plane, same lockers, with nothing added, said Glezer, of Consumer Champion. “They’ve made free space scarce and now charge you for a headstart.” It’s also a reminder that getting on a plane headed for Bali (nearly synonymous with the Jetstar brand) provides little respite from the reminder of inequality (extra fees, priority boarding, The Chairman’s Lounge) that somehow make the experience of the cost-of-living crisis worse. Perhaps for this reason, when asked about Jetstar’s change, Victoria’s newly minted premier, Ben Carroll, gave a revealing comment, suggesting almost a resignation with the airlines. While he opposed Jetstar’s new fee, Carroll said: “Having been with my family on a Jetstar flight recently, can I say I’m not surprised?

Advertisement

“It was hard enough getting on and having to pay for your coffee and everything else,” Carroll told ABC radio. And yet, as Jetstar was quick to point out, they didn’t come up with the idea of charging for priority access to the overhead bins. Loading This is unfortunately the norm in Europe, where the profitable airlines are the cheapest. Ireland-based Ryanair, which does a booming business, developed, under chief executive Michael O’Leary, a business model that establishes that if you want anything more than your seat, you have to pay extra. Jetstar seems to be heading down the same path.

Advertisement

UNSW senior aviation lecturer Ian Douglas said the new Jetstar fee is “pretty much consistent with all the carriers in Europe”. Douglas said that for many European airlines, the airfares don’t cover total operating costs. “It’s the ancillary revenues from bags, seat assignments, loyalty programs that get the total industry to profit.” Ancillary fees for baggage and seat selection made up almost a third of Ryanair’s €15.54 billion ($25.5 billion) revenue in the past financial year. Ancillary revenue share ranges from a mere 3 per cent for full-service carriers to 62 per cent for ultra-low-cost airlines, according to airline retail and revenue strategy company IdeaWorksCompany, quoted in Forbes. It will be cold comfort that Qantas-owned Jetstar occupies a unique place as one of the few successful low-cost carriers owned by a national premium carrier.

There was something very familiar about SpaceX’s first quarterly result as a listed company. A near-doubling of revenue was swamped by a massive increase in spending.
