Getty SpaceX’s capex leapt from $US2.8 billion in the same quarter last year and $US10.1 billion in the March quarter to a whopping $US18.4 billion, with the company flagging it will remain at about that same rate for the rest of the year. That would mean capex of about $US65 billion this year. While SpaceX isn’t a pure artificial intelligence play – it also has its profitable Starlink satellite business and its unprofitable Starship rockets – that broad narrative of explosive revenue growth being overwhelmed by the scale of investment is consistent throughout the AI sector.

Advertisement

Critical to the fate of AI, or at least of those US companies pursuing their costly proprietary advanced AI models, is whether the trillions of dollars they are investing will ever generate a return commensurate with that investment and its inherent risk. At this point in the sector’s development, that remains an open question. Revenue from AI is up about 250 per cent. But the capex driving that revenue growth is up by more than 550 per cent. SpaceX is generating revenue growth beyond market expectations, including growth in its AI revenues, which have risen from $US737 million in the June quarter last year to $US818 million in the first quarter of this year and then to $US2.6 billion in the latest June quarter. So, revenue from AI is up about 250 per cent. But the capex driving that revenue growth is up by more than 550 per cent. Moreover, SpaceX’s sales growth isn’t coming purely from selling AI products to customers, but rather from selling access to its AI infrastructure. The company is selling “compute” – processing power – to Google for $US920 million a month, and to Anthropic for $US1.25 billion a month.

Advertisement

As for the rest of the AI sector, the future for SpaceX’s AI business is cloudy, with the only near-term likelihood that its losses – $US1.26 billion in the latest quarter and $US2 billion for the first half of this year – will continue to mount. Related Article Opinion

Sharemarket Brave new world: SpaceX is now the most expensive stock on the planet Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Elon Musk, of course, remains super confident. He says he expects the “cadence” of AI development to improve dramatically and the company to end this year with 2GW of capacity and “closer to 10GW of compute than 5GW of compute” next year. He also believes SpaceX’s overall revenue base is about to explode. The June quarter revenues, annualised, produce a run-rate of just over $US30 billion for the financial year. By 2030, he says, he expects revenues to reach $US1 trillion – a year earlier than his earlier projections. Indeed, there was a “non-zero probability” that the $US1 trillion mark could be achieved in 2029, he said.

Advertisement

To get there by 2030 – which would require an annual compound growth rate in revenues of about 140 per cent – AI will have to be central for the company, but it won’t all be about AI. The only profitable business in SpaceX’s portfolio at this stage is its Starlink satellite business, which had revenue of $US4.3 billion (up from $US2.6 billion a year earlier) and generated a profit of $US1.66 billion. Starlink now has 12 million subscribers, double the level of a year ago. That satellite business might soon be complemented with a wireless service, which will send shudders through the senior ranks of AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile, whose share prices all fell on the news. SpaceX said it will acquire spectrum and build the terrestrial infrastructure that will enable Starlink to offer a direct-to-mobile service. As for the rest of the AI sector, the future for SpaceX’s AI business is cloudy, with the only near-term likelihood that its losses will continue to mount. Critical to Musk’s vision of data centres in space and the colonisation of Mars (and strengthening Starlink’s coverage and capabilities) is the space business, in which SpaceX invested $US1.2 billion during the quarter, and which generated revenue from its Starship launches of $US962 million.

Advertisement

Starship’s giant reusable rockets, while having had a troubled gestation, would dramatically reduce the cost of launching payloads, and people, into space and are the key to SpaceX’s ability to build those orbiting data centres, powered by the sun, and eventually putting people on Mars. SpaceX, which launched two Starship V3 test flights earlier this year, says Starship “continued to advance towards full and rapid reusability.” Elon Musk’s SpaceX is burning through cash. AP The underlying questionmark over all Musk’s ambitions is whether he will run out of cash before he realises them. The cash burn at SpaceX is significant and accelerating. The initial public offering in June, which raised about $US85 billion, may have left the group with net cash of $US93.5 billion, but the AI and Starship programs will rapidly diminish that cash pile.

Advertisement

There have been reports that Musk is considering the sale of Tesla’s China operations as a prelude to a merger of SpaceX and Tesla, which has more than $US40 billion of cash, but Musk wasn’t drawn on the merger question in the analyst briefing for SpaceX’s results. There is, however, a significant amount of overlap between SpaceX and the increasingly AI-centric Tesla, and the market expects Musk’s two listed vehicles to eventually merge. Whether that would resolve, or at least delay, a need for new SpaceX funding is uncertain, given that Tesla, too, is significantly ramping up its capex and spending on AI. While most of the analysts who follow SpaceX (many of whom work for banks involved in the IPO) remain wildly bullish about SpaceX’s prospects – and SpaceX did beat almost all their forecasts, other than their big miss on capex – the wider market is a little less certain. Shares in the IPO were offered at $US135 each and, post-listing, initially soared to $US225. They closed at about $US125 on Tuesday, before tumbling more than 8 per cent – at one point they were down by about $US11 a share – after the market closed. SpaceX has lost more than $US1 trillion of market value from its peak.

Advertisement

And there may be more losses to come. On Thursday in the US, about 911.5 million shares that were in lock-up before the quarterly’s release, will be available for trading. Related Article Opinion

AI Scared by tech’s debt deluge, investors are questioning the AI boom Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist That compares with the 640 million currently available, accounting for roughly 5 per cent of SpaceX’s issued capital. It could have been even more, had SpaceX shares continued to trade at elevated prices, with the release of a further 455 million dependent on the company hitting share price thresholds. The 911.5 million shares are a giant over-hang on the shares, and short-sellers have been queuing up in anticipation, with positions equivalent to more than a third of the shares currently available for trading. While the IPO’s aftermarket might have been disappointing – and costly, for those who subscribed to the IPO, who could still face a rocky few days, weeks or months – SpaceX still has a market capitalisation of about $US1.7 trillion.

Advertisement

That is pretty impressive for an unprofitable, capital-devouring company and an indicator of the market’s faith in Musk, his fantastical visions and the eventual (and necessarily unprecedented, given the sheer scale of the investments) profit-generating potential of AI. title: Libertarian MP demands ICAC hearing be halted, calls for inquiry into ‘leaking’
text:
Advertisement

Follow our live coverage of the inquiry here. A NSW MP has called for the Independent Commission Against Corruption’s bombshell examination of illegal donations to be paused pending an inquiry into whether the watchdog has been leaking information to the media. John Ruddick, a Libertarian Party member of the NSW upper house, claimed in parliament on Wednesday that Operation Rosny “appears to be tainted” because the Herald has revealed several details about the key players targeted by the ICAC over recent weeks. Ruddick wants the Inspector-General of the ICAC, Gail Furness, SC, to investigate whether ICAC staff had disclosed information in a potential breach of the law, and also demanded parliament order an independent inquiry into his claims. He offered no evidence to support his allegations, other than that the Herald’s coverage has referenced sources who are unauthorised to speak publicly.

Advertisement

The ICAC began its investigation in mid-2022 into the links between the NSW Liberal Party, fugitive Sydney developer Jean Nassif, Catholic Schools NSW and several other figures, including from the Labor Party. Operation Rosny is due to hold eight weeks of public hearings. Related Article Live

Operation Rosny ICAC Operation Rosny LIVE updates: Jean-Claude Perrottet begins evidence as inquiry enters eighth day Ruddick is particularly focused on a story by the Herald late last month which revealed names on the witness list for the first week of hearings. Ruddick has repeatedly suggested on social media platform X that the ICAC staff leaked the document. However, the witness list was widely circulated to parties involved in Operation Rosny before the Herald obtained and published the document. Ruddick told parliament it should condemn “any attempt by a financially desperate, taxpayer-supported media organisation to weaponise confidential ICAC processes or interfere with the integrity of public hearings for its own commercial or political ends”.

Advertisement

He cited stories from more than a decade ago to support his claim the Herald has used confidential sources to report on matters involving the ICAC. On July 30, a solicitor for the ICAC, Roy Walden, emailed Ruddick to say it had been made aware of “comments by you on X, in which you alleged that ‘operatives within the ICAC are leaking to the SMH on an industrial scale’.” Walden said in his email that he was not aware of any evidence that any commission officer has “leaked” information in relation to Operation Rosny. Walden also said if Ruddick had any evidence of misconduct by ICAC staff it should be referred to Furness in her capacity as the inspector of the ICAC. Meanwhile, Jean-Claude Perrottet, the 29-year-old brother of former premier Dominic Perrottet, told the commission on Wednesday he was “let go” from his job at Catholic Schools NSW in June, just one month after being promoted.

Advertisement

Perrottet, a key member of the right-wing Catholic group the Reformers which is at the centre of the corruption inquiry, confirmed he was made redundant from the education body just weeks before Operation Rosny was announced. Catholic Schools NSW chief executive Dallas McInerney is also a person of interest to ICAC. Jean-Claude Perrottet gives evidence at the corruption inquiry. ICAC This commission is investigating whether Jean-Claude Perrottet solicited unlawful donations from prohibited donors. One of those was hotelier Michael O’Hara. It is also probing whether McInerney approved donations from Catholic Schools NSW to the Liberal Party, via the Reformers. “I want to suggest to you, Mr Perrottet, that the reason you were made redundant only a month after you’ve been promoted to this new role was because of your involvement in this inquiry. Is that right?” counsel assisting Juliet Curtin asked Perrottet. “That wasn’t what was communicated to me from the office and the emails that I received. But I mean, obviously, I’ve thought about the timing of it,” he responded.

Advertisement

Senior NSW Liberal MP Damien Tudehope conceded on Tuesday he had leaked a confidential draft report from a parliamentary inquiry to a key witness who deliberately avoided giving evidence, in a stunning revelation that could threaten the party elder’s political future. Tudehope, then the Coalition government’s most senior member of the upper house, sent the 2023 confidential report into illegal donations and the Hills Shire Council to lobbyist and Liberal Party operative Jeremy Greenwood, the Independent Commission Against Corruption heard on Tuesday. Greenwood was one of four Liberal apparatchiks who hid or fled overseas to avoid being handed a summons to appear before the parliamentary inquiry, which was one of the catalysts for the broader ICAC probe. Liberal leader Kellie Sloane has said the Tudehope revelation was not acceptable. But she left open the possibility he could return to her frontbench after the inquiry, saying yesterday’s evidence had “not changed my position about keeping Damien on the backbench for the short term”. The Herald revealed last week that Liberal MP Chris Rath was captured by a wiretap helping party apparatchiks evade the statewide manhunt to force them before the parliamentary probe.

title: Victoria Hannan’s marriage ended at 28 with a text message. It marked a new beginning
text:
Advertisement

LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life Victoria Hannan’s marriage ended at 28 with a text message. It marked a new beginning Victoria Hannan August 5, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I separated from my husband not long after Eat Pray Love came out. By the time the divorce was finalised a year later, I had, against my will, acquired three copies of Elizabeth Gilbert’s divorce memoir. One arrived anonymously in the mail. Two others were slid across cafe tables by friends who looked at me with the sort of expression people usually reserve for the recently bereaved. If you’re one of the few who missed the Eat Pray Love phenomenon, the premise was simple enough: God comes to Elizabeth Gilbert on the floor of her bathroom after hours of praying and gives her the confirmation she needs to leave her husband, so she destroys her marriage and reconstructs herself overseas. Italy for appetite. India for spirituality. Bali for love. When she divorced at 28, author Victoria Hannan felt a freedom, but also a powerful uncertainty. This kind of drama is the lifeblood of a divorce narrative: marriage-ending equals world-ending. There’s also a factoid that people quote with alarming solemnity: that divorce, moving house and death are life’s three greatest stressors. My own divorce, however, felt less like catastrophe and more like admin. There were no lawyers. No custody arrangements. No dramatic division of money or real estate. I was 28 years old and our shared assets amounted to one large IKEA saucepan and a collection of Curb Your Enthusiasm DVDs.

Advertisement

I got the saucepan. We had been together since we were 20. Married for four years. The marriage did not end because anybody committed some unforgivable act. It ended because somewhere along the way I began to feel fixed in place. I remember worrying too much about the wedding gifts. Would his old boss want the juicer back? At 27, I had started to feel as though I was trapped inside an earlier version of myself. The person I had been at 20 was still making decisions for me. There were things I wanted to do, ways I wanted to live and selves I wanted to try on. I could not work out whether growth inside a marriage was possible when the marriage itself had been built when we were so young. Now that I’m in a healthy relationship that supports change, I know this growth is possible. But at 27, I lacked the language for any of this.

Advertisement

Nobody tells you how to get divorced, especially when so young. We were the first of our friends to marry and both our sets of parents were still together. We had no earthly idea what was supposed to happen next. (I’ve often thought there should be a small bureaucratic clause in your marriage certificate: In the event of dissolution, do not panic. This happens all the time!) My reference points for divorce were Elizabeth Gilbert and Elizabeth Taylor: one made divorce appear spiritually transformative, the other made it look glamorous. Mine was neither. Nothing was dramatically wrong. My husband was kind. There was no betrayal, no event I could pinpoint to justify dismantling a life. If anything, this just made the divorce feel faintly embarrassing. Julia Roberts played Elizabeth Gilbert in the film version of Eat Pray Love. We had stood in front of our friends and families and announced, with absolute confidence, that this arrangement would last forever. Then, four years later, our pledge was quietly redacted. I remember worrying too much about the wedding gifts. Would his old boss want the juicer back? At the time, this seemed as pressing a concern as the emotional collapse of the marriage itself.

Advertisement

By the time we officially separated, we were already living in different cities and leading separate lives with increasing competence. The divorce itself happened almost entirely via paperwork in Australia while we were living in the UK. Nobody appeared in court. At one point, my ex-husband phoned someone to confirm the paperwork had gone through, then he texted me. And that was that. A marriage over in a text message. Related Article Sunday Life Five years after I had a ‘COVID baby’, these words from a psychologist still break me Afterwards, I found myself trying out different performances of a young divorcee. My instinct was to make a joke of it by referring to it as my “first divorce”, like it was no big deal. But it was a big deal. It was desperately sad, and it made me feel ashamed. I had made a public declaration and then failed to uphold it. But as time passed – and my therapy sessions increased – I was able to start to reframe it. What if the divorce was not the tragedy? What if the tragedy had been remaining exactly where I was? Because with the shame came a powerful sense of uncertainty (and hope) about the shape the future held. Suddenly, I felt free from the exhausting pressure of trying to force permanence onto something that no longer fit. I felt relief from the idea that staying was inherently more virtuous than leaving.

Advertisement

We tend to see marriage as success and divorce as failure because culturally we remain deeply invested in endurance as a moral achievement. But sometimes ending a marriage is the hopeful act.

I didn’t speak to God, I didn’t go to an ashram or have my life changed by a plate of spaghetti. What I experienced instead was quieter. It was the sense that my life had become, once again, unwritten. And with my pen in hand, I was ready to start again. I Love the Whole World! title: Stokes on booze, Baz, next year’s Ashes and his ambition to coach England
text:
Advertisement

SportEngland Stokes on booze, Baz, next year’s Ashes and his ambition to coach England Will Macpherson August 5, 2026 — 11:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Key points Former England cricket captain Ben Stokes told his former teammates Stuart Broad and Jos Butler on their podcast that he doesn’t believe his team had a drinking problem, but he does think the sport’s relationship with alcohol has not moved with the times.

The all-rounder dismissed suggestions he would return to the England Test team as a player, but said he wanted to one day coach his country.

Stokes said he was surprised his vice-captain Harry Brook was not appointed as his replacement as Test captain and had concerns about his good friend Joe Root returning to the role.

The podcast heard Stokes wrote an uncommissioned report into England’s dismal Ashes campaign last Australian summer.

Stokes also spoke about his relationships with outgoing Test coach Brendon McCullum and England cricket director Rob Key.

Ben Stokes believes cricket’s relationship with alcohol has not “moved on” as the game has become more professional but denied the England team he captained had a drinking problem. Stokes ended a 15-year international career in June when his Test side lost to New Zealand, but is continuing to play for his boyhood county Durham. England captain Ben Stokes leaves the field at Trent Bridge after his final innings. Getty Speaking in-depth for the first time since retiring in Nottingham, Stokes appeared on For The Love of Cricket, the podcast hosted by his friends and former teammates Stuart Broad and Jos Buttler. Stokes was asked directly by Broad if his team had a drinking problem, following a series of late-night episodes over the past year, headlined by Harry Brook being punched by a bouncer in Wellington, hours before captaining England in an ODI before the Ashes.

Advertisement

Stokes refuted the allegation: “No … that is such an extreme thing to put on a team. “But I think cricket has a drinking culture and that has not changed. We are in 2026 now, where the game has gone more professional over the years. But one thing that has just stayed within cricket is its relationship with alcohol, from club cricket it works its way up. It stays there and is embedded within the sport. Loading “That is the relationship between alcohol and cricket, it has not moved on as the game has become more professional. There’s more science and medicine, more nutritional information, more this and that. One thing that has been a constant, and has been for a very long time, is the relationship with alcohol. For people who think the English cricket team has a drinking culture, I would say no. I would just say cricket has a culture that is associated with alcohol.” Stokes has had an up and down relationship with alcohol across his career. In 2017 he was arrested for a brawl in Bristol while drunk after an ODI against West Indies, was found not guilty of affray and later gave up alcohol. After England beat New Zealand at Lord’s in June, he went out and was accused of breaking the team’s curfew.

Advertisement

“I think it [cricket’s relationship with alcohol] can be a problem,” he said. Related Article England Bazball apology: McCullum owns up for failed England experiment “If you look at everything over the years, a lot of people who have been involved within cricket, have had bad relationships with alcohol. I don’t know what you do to change it. It’s just one of those things that … I have had, I don’t want to say problems, but I’ve had relationships with alcohol over my career that have been potentially dangerous, if that makes sense. But that is completely different to me now. “There is a relationship with alcohol that has been the same since the 1980s, as the game has got better and better, that has stayed around.” However, Stokes said he did not regret his decision to take his team for a mid-Ashes trip to the Queensland seaside resort of Noosa last summer, despite scrutiny of their drinking there.

Advertisement

Ashes prospects There has been much speculation, including from managing director Rob Key, that Stokes could return for next year’s Ashes. He has continued to shut this down, and described himself as “definitely” retired. Stokes also spoke about how, aged 35, he could not envisage playing on under another captain, unlike his predecessors Root and Alastair Cook, who were both 31 when they stepped down from the captaincy. The snubbing of Brook Root has already done a five-year stint as captain before Stokes, but has been installed alongside the new Test coach, Stephen Fleming. Brook will remain in charge of the white-ball side with Brendon McCullum as coach. Key, the managing director, said the Test role had come “too soon” for Brook, who is 27.

Advertisement

“I think just if you think someone’s going to be a good captain or a good leader, then just give them it,” Stokes said. “Brooky was made vice-captain – I’m not there any more, but even when I missed that Test match, I was like: ‘He’s vice-captain?’ I sort of understood the reasoning why they were saying it, but what message is that sending to him? Ben Stokes thought his deputy, Harry Brook, should’ve assumed the England capataincy once he retired. ECB via Getty Images “He’s vice-captain, and the captain is not playing, but he’s not captain. And then the same again here [with the permanent role].” Stokes expressed concern about Root, a close confidant, doing the job after the toll it took during his first stint between 2017 and 2022.

Advertisement

“I love Rooty and I wish him nothing but success,” he said. “I hope he achieves amazing things in his role as captain. He’s going to really enjoy working with Flem. He’s a great man, I’ve worked with him before. I told Joe, I said my only worry is just you. “And that’s all I really care about now, just because I have seen what he went through and how much he put himself through [last time as captain]. “He’s just always put the team first, like he always comes second. And that’s just my only concern with it is just obviously knowing what he went through last time he was in charge of the team because I don’t want to see that ever happen again because I care for Joe a lot, but I wish him all the success in the world.” Coaching ambitions

Advertisement

Stokes has taken tentative first steps in coaching in the Hundred, with England Lions and the Durham academy, but has set his sights on coaching England. “I’m doing my level three coaching [course] now while I’m still playing because I want, when the day comes that I’m not playing any more, I’d love to be able to have all that stuff signed off and done,” he said. “I know what I want to do in terms of staying within the game, which is to be a coach. “And would I love to be coach of England one day? Absolutely. I just really like the idea of being in some form of leadership away from playing.” Ben Stokes has returned to his county, Durham, since retiring from international duty. Getty Images England’s Ashes review

Advertisement

Stokes confirmed that he provided a written a review of England’s Ashes campaign, despite not being asked for an official report. “I just found it interesting and weird that maybe that’s never happened before,” he said. “Maybe a captain’s never really been [asked], ‘can you give us your official [thoughts]’ ... so I was like, stuff it, I’m going to do anyway. I was writing stuff down.” Ben Stokes and Brendon McCullum led the England Test team for four years. Getty Images He said his wife, Claire, and mother-in-law helped him write the report and he made sure it was right “in terms of structure and spelling” because “I didn’t want to do it half-a---- because it was such a big thing for me”. The response was a “good meeting” with Key and McCullum, who all remained in their job initially. Six months on, only Key survives. Stokes expressed surprise that McCullum was sacked as Test coach, saying his relationship with the coach remained strong despite reports of tactical divergence during the Ashes.

Advertisement

Related Article Exclusive

Australian cricket ‘Pretty annoying’: Inside Josh Hazlewood’s fight to keep his Test career alive When it came to the Rex Rooms incident that he admits contributed to the end of his career, Stokes said he was “not here to go into all that detail”. He described it as a “sticky situation for quite a few people involved”. “There’s a time and a place for that,” he said. “And now isn’t that time because I don’t want to come across bitter towards anyone yet because I’m chilled right now.“

title: Secret missions and staged meetings: How a backroom deal led to IBAC probe
text:
Advertisement

Updated PoliticsVictoriaIBAC Secret missions and staged meetings: How a backroom deal led to IBAC probe Kieran Rooney Updated August 5, 2026 — 11:55am ,first published August 5, 2026 — 9:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An eight-year-long investigation into negotiations between the Andrews government and the firefighters’ union has found “serious and concerning conduct” by Victorian ministers, MPs and public servants. The findings were contained in Operation Richmond, an investigation led by the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission (IBAC) that began in 2018, and which was suppressed for years by legal challenges, despite the watchdog’s efforts to have it made public. Operation Richmond centred on dealings between Daniel Andrews’ government and the United Firefighters Union under Peter Marshall. Marija Ercegovac Tabled in parliament on Wednesday, the IBAC report identified serious issues in the way pay deals with the Country Fire Authority (CFA) and the Metropolitan Fire Brigade (MFB) were negotiated alongside the establishment of Fire Rescue Victoria. However, it stopped short of finding corrupt conduct – for which Victoria has a higher threshold than any other state. “IBAC found that senior members of government acted contrary to established policies, procedures, codes of conduct and conventions in negotiating a deal with the secretary of the United Firefighters Union [UFU], Mr Peter Marshall, for the CFA Enterprise Bargaining Agreement [EBA] without the knowledge and involvement of the responsible minister, agencies and department,” Commissioner Victoria Elliott said at the start of the report.

Advertisement

“By doing so, the government placed itself in a position where Mr Marshall was able to exert extraordinary influence over the negotiations for both the CFA EBA and the MFB EBA.” The report covers a period when Daniel Andrews was premier of Victoria. The CFA pay deal became a political flashpoint for his government, and the late Jane Garrett resigned as emergency services minister and quit cabinet because she disagreed with her government’s moves to accept UFU demands. “The government placed itself in a position where Mr Marshall was able to exert extraordinary influence.” Delayed Operation Richmond report “During the period investigated, IBAC also found that Mr Marshall was afforded privileged access to senior members of government which, in many cases, were not disclosed and were to the exclusion of other key stakeholders,” the report said. “Operation Richmond highlights how government leaders, including ministers and the premier, can undermine established checks and balances when they fail to model high integrity standards and act as stewards of good governance.”

Advertisement

The report was originally scheduled for release by the end of June, but was delayed by an unsuccessful legal challenge from Marshall. Related Article IBAC Firefighters’ union boss loses court battle to bury corruption investigation, but appeal possible Operation Richmond began after IBAC received allegations that Marshall had blackmailed or compromised the premier to change his position on the 2016 CFA pay deal. The blackmail claim was never substantiated. The investigation was widened to include negotiations for a pay deal with the Metropolitan Fire Brigade and the creation of its replacement, Fire Rescue Victoria. Ultimately, it found that in 2016 Andrews authorised then special minister of state Gavin Jennings, with the assistance of Tony Bates – a deputy secretary at the Department of Premier and Cabinet – to negotiate the CFA deal directly without the knowledge of the CFA themselves.

Advertisement

“While in negotiations on 11 April 2016, Minister Jennings referred to being ‘off doing my secret mission’ and ‘secret business’ in text messages to staff in his office and the PPO [Premier’s Private Office],” the report said. “Private meetings were held with the UFU in rented meeting spaces and a hotel. Those involved were instructed to keep the meetings confidential.” After four days of negotiations, the two sides agreed to terms and Jennings texted Andrews: “Handshake has occurred – it’s done!” Once these negotiations were finished, IBAC found, a document outlining the terms was presented to cabinet as a proposal from the union, with ministers – including Garrett – unaware they had been negotiated with people inside government. Marshall summarised these meetings years later in an intercepted phone call from 2019, where the UFU chief told a ministerial adviser the pay deal was “was negotiated with f---in’ Jennings in a back room. It was endorsed by f---in’ Andrews and cabinet.”

Advertisement

On April 13, 2016, Marshall met with Andrews and a staffer for what IBAC viewed as a staged event so that there could be a witness to the agreement being presented to government as a “proposal” from the union. Evidence from Bates appeared to support this assessment. The senior public servant told investigators he led the development of the deal and “if there was a presentation of the agreement to the premier’s office I would categorise it as ceremonial”. Even after cabinet’s expenditure committee signed off on the deal on April 19, Garrett and the CFA remained opposed to it. Garrett told IBAC she was contacted by a federal Labor senator to persuade her to progress the deal with the Fair Work Commission.

Advertisement

The CFA agreed to return to the commission in May and resume conciliation, but Marshall resisted any attempts to compromise on the EBA and would not budge on the veto clauses. On May 23, the premier sent a text message to Jennings asking how mediation was progressing. Jennings responded: “At 11am he [Marshall] was convinced you were a treacherous c--- and I was a f---ing idiot ... By lunchtime he was giving me the benefit of the doubt.” Firefighters’ union chief Peter Marshall on the steps of the Victorian Parliament in 2022. Chris Hopkins The IBAC report said evidence gathered through Operation Richmond showed Andrews wanted to end the pay dispute in a way that excluded Garrett, then emergency services minister, whom he didn’t believe could resolve the matter. “At the time of the decision, the premier was facing internal political pressure, negative media attention and industrial unrest,” the report said.

Advertisement

But IBAC found that in secretly excluding Garrett, the CFA and other key parts of government from the process, the premier, Jennings and Bates had behaved contrary to “government policy, procedures, convention and their respective codes of conduct”. Related Article IBAC Damning IBAC report exposes influence of Peter Marshall and firefighters union It also found the undisclosed negotiations limited the state’s bargaining position and their ability to resist Marshall’s demands. A key concern among those who did not support the deal were clauses that required the CFA to “consult and agree” with the UFU on decisions before they could be made. They became known as “veto clauses”, which effectively allowed the union to increase its control of the CFA by blocking policies it did not agree with.

Advertisement

Garrett quit cabinet in June 2016 because she considered the pay deal unacceptable, and when the CFA board refused to endorse the agreement they were stood down and replaced. Their successors signed off on the arrangement. At the same time, Marshall expected the terms of the CFA deal to be replicated in a pay deal with the Metropolitan Fire Brigade. One former MFB chief executive told IBAC that they had concerns similar to the CFA’s, including that some elements of the deal were unlawful or undermined safety obligations. “Ultimately, to resolve the dispute, the government appointed new members to the MFB board who understood the government’s preferred position on the MFB EBA [enterprise bargaining agreement],” the report said. IBAC also raised concerns about the way a 2019 bill that reformed the fire services was passed – which ultimately turned the MFB and the paid parts of the CFA into a new body named Fire Rescue Victoria.

Advertisement

The corruption watchdog found Marshall had sought to secure the support of a crossbench MP by hiring their relative days before it was due for a vote in the upper house. title: Jetstar’s new overhead baggage rules explained: When they start and what you'll pay
text:
In brief Jetstar will charge between $25 and $52 for carry-on bags stored in overhead lockers from February 2027.

New size-based baggage rules scrap routine weighing and offer priority boarding for paying travellers.

Storing carry-on baggage in overhead lockers on Jetstar flights will cost up to $52 one-way, as the budget airline announces new charges for passengers.

Jetstar chief executive Stephanie Tully says the changes to the airline's carry-on baggage allowances will streamline boarding and help more flights depart on time.

"Our new carry-on baggage model provides more choice to customers while helping to keep our fares low," Tully added.

"You only pay for what you need — travelling with less means paying less, and you can always add more if you need."

The changes follow "extensive research and feedback from customers and crew" which found frustrations with weighing bags and finding enough room in overhead lockers, Jetstar said.

Cabin baggage scales used to weigh passengers' carry-on bags before boarding will no longer be "routinely" used, the airline said.

title: Low-income families call for support as national reading, writing school results slip
text:
In brief One in three students missed basic NAPLAN benchmarks as reading scores fell across all year levels.

Families of children needing extra support say results can be demoralising.

Ruby and her 11-year-old son Mark were dreading the day his scores on the national school assessment program were released.

And they confirmed the family's worst fears: despite working hard to learn, the Year 5 student remained behind his peers.

Mark, whose name the Australian Associated Press agreed not to publish, was one of more than 1.3 million children in Years 3, 5, 7, and 9 who sat the National Assessment Program — Literacy and Numeracy (NAPLAN) in 2026.

As the only standardised national assessment, NAPLAN was primarily designed to help governments and schools measure results and fix funding or teaching shortfalls.

But for students such as Mark, seeing their results can be demoralising.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

He has ADHD and autism and needs extra support at school.

"When I got the results, because it comes under Mark's name, he wanted to see his results,'' Ruby said.

"In his reading column ... it actually said the bottom, bottom.

"I just thought to myself, 'How could it be right at the bottom when he's improved so much?'"

READ MORE Pioneering Australian school aims to prove there's more to education than NAPLAN

But scores for reading were worse than in 2025 for every year level, and Year 5 students were the only cohort whose writing ability had improved.

Overall, about one in three students across all levels did not meet basic literacy and numeracy benchmarks, falling into "developing" and "needs additional support" categories.

The writing scores were a particular concern in the two lowest grades tested, with less than 10 per cent of students exceeding national benchmarks.

Numeracy results had improved for most cohorts since 2025, though Year 3's score had decreased.

Results from previous years showed a clear literacy divide between children from wealthy, educated areas and those who grow up in areas of low socio-economic status.

Ruby said she also struggled at school and her challenges went unnoticed because of her learning environment.

She is now raising her children on a low income.

"With Mark, I just wish there was more people, just more at the school to help," she said.

Better support that understands the specific needs of struggling families would help improve results, The Smith Family chief executive Doug Taylor said.

"With 72,000 low-income students across Australia, the right support at the right time can make a huge difference," he said, noting schools should also consider the skills students had beyond academic ones.

In rural communities and towns with high Indigenous populations, results have dramatically improved in recent years.

That was due to increased funding and the use of explicit teaching models, Education Minister Jason Clare said in a speech at the Garma Indigenous festival over the weekend.

"Over the last four years, the numeracy results of Indigenous students have gone up and up,'' he said.

"In Year 5 by 9.5 points and in Year 7 by 9.3 points. That's a good sign."

Separately, the federal government's commitment to cover a quarter of the Schooling Resource Standard to reach full funding for public schools was rolled out in 2026.

In October, the controversial Thriving Kids program will, in part, replace the National Disability Insurance Scheme for children under nine with development delays.

Tasmanian students did not sit NAPLAN in 2026 because of industrial action.

title: 2026 Census: The new questions on gender and sexual orientation explained
text:
IN BRIEF Two new questions have been added to the Census about gender identity and sexual orientation.

A question on ancestry has been expanded to allow up to four responses.

The Census of Population and Housing has long tracked a changing Australia — but for more than a century, a piece of the nation's story has been missing, LGBTIQ+ Health Australia CEO Nicky Bath says.

Bath says the organisation has been calling for the addition of questions regarding sexual orientation, gender identification and expression.

"I remember in the run-up to the 2021 Census being contacted by older people who thought that they wouldn't be alive for the 2026 Census, and it was very sad for them that they wouldn't be able to participate ... in this way," she told SBS News.

What are the new Census questions?

The 2026 Census will now include two new questions about gender and sexual orientation.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Respondents will still be asked about their sex recorded at birth, but people over the age of 16 can also specify their gender as male, female, non-binary or another term.

An optional question regarding sexual orientation has been added, with answers including straight, gay or lesbian, bisexual or an open-ended response for another term.

Why is the Census collecting this information?

Bath said Census data — which will be released in three phases starting from June 2027 — will inform the availability, funding and location of LGBTQI+ community and health services.

If people in Australia do not complete the Census they can be fined up to $364 a day. Credit: ABS

"The decision has been a long time coming ... for many people, being able to mark those boxes in the Census is really important with regards to validation and for us to be seen as important members of the community. That's a really important historical moment."

What wasn't included in the new questions?

Advocates like Equality Australia say the number of people living in houseboats has been recorded in the Census for decades, but LGBTQI+ populations have not been traced.

Anna Brown, CEO of Equality Australia, said Census data collected about LGBTQI+ people would be "transformative".

"We're really looking forward to learning just how many LGBTQ+ people there are in Australia, because we know that if we aren't counted, we remain invisible in the data that shapes decisions about our lives," she told SBS News.

"Better data leads to better decisions on health, housing, education, aged care, and community services. Until now, governments have been making these decisions without a complete picture of our communities."

Brown has also called for Australians with innate variations of sex characteristics or intersex people to be counted by the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).

"We will continue to advocate for its inclusion and work with the ABS ... towards recommending that this population be included," she said.

Census questions are informed by the 2020 ABS standards for sex, gender, variations in sex characteristics, and sexual orientation variables. These standards specify that: "The inclusion of born with a variation of sex characteristics or intersex as a response option in a sex question ... is not capable of generating reliable or consistent results in measuring this population, and perpetuates the misconception that intersex people are neither male nor female."

Bath said more work is needed to ensure Australians are educated about innate variations of sex characteristics, which she believes is often "conflated with sex and gender".

However, she is choosing to view Census outcomes with a glass "half full" approach.

READ MORE Agency behind Australian census admits there was a problem with 'non-binary' question

"We know that there are challenges with not having the gender question being asked to people who are under 16. That means that people with trans and gender diverse children are not going to be able to inform the Census about their children.

"On the other side of that, though, we will get data for the first time on people who are over 16, and that is very, very important," Brown said.

What else has changed in the 2026 Census?

Jenny Telford, general manager of the Census and Population division at the ABS, said answers have also been expanded to reflect the "rich cultural makeup across the country".

Previously, an ancestry question, which gathered data on people's lineage or descent, only allowed up to two response options. Now, respondents can provide up to four answers.

Telford said the change will provide "richer insights into the cultural makeup of every area across Australia".

Jenny Telford, general manager of the Census and Population division at the ABS, said the Census provides critical data on "who we are and how we are changing over time". Credit: ABS

Peter Doukas is the chair of the Federation of Ethnic Communities Councils of Australia, the peak body representing Australians from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds.

"We were very much in support of the ancestry data being added to [the Census] and I think we're going to see some very interesting results in terms of not only people from a non-English-speaking or cultural background, but also from First Nations backgrounds," he told SBS News.

The ABS has announced it aims to better reflect Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultural identity.

"So getting a good count of our Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander population in the 2026 Census is a really important priority for the ABS," Telford said.

"We've expanded things like the languages that people can report on the Census form to include more Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages than we've had in the past."

On 11 August, the ABS will also ask people how they travelled to work. The Census has updated its response category to include a new bicycle option (including e-bike) to reflect what it described as "more contemporary modes of travel".

title: As allies desert FIFA boss Gianni Infantino, is there anyone ready to replace him?
text:
In brief Key allies continue to turn on FIFA president Gianni Infantino.

His plan to privatise parts of the World Cup has exploded into one of football's biggest controversies in years.

Pressure on FIFA president Gianni Infantino has intensified, with opposition emerging both within world football's governing body and from external critics over his since-abandoned proposal to open the World Cup to private investment.

Former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger, appointed in 2019 by Infantino as FIFA's chief of global football development, said in a statement on Tuesday that "the decision to withdraw the project was absolutely necessary and beyond question".

His remarks followed hot on the heels of an extraordinary internal email to FIFA staff, seen by the Agence France-Presse (AFP) news agency, in which secretary-general Mattias Grafstrom appeared to distance himself from Infantino on the issue.

Previously seen as close to Infantino, Grafstrom describes the fiasco surrounding the plan as "a sad and reproachable series of events".

FIFA floated the plan last Tuesday, saying it could raise up to US$4.2 billion ($5.95 billion) of private investment based on a valuation of US$20 billion ($28 billion) for a new commercial subsidiary, called the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), which it proposed would handle commercial rights for events such as the World Cup and Club World Cup.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

By Saturday, it was dead in the water, as Infantino announced he was abandoning the plan after widespread condemnation, with European governing body UEFA having threatened to boycott all FIFA competitions, including the World Cup.

Far from calming the waters or shoring up his presidency, Infantino has been swamped with criticism of his leadership style; the previously smooth path to being re-elected unopposed for a fourth and final term next March now looks rocky.

'Take immediate steps'

However, re-election is a problem down the road. For now, Infantion has others to confront.

Even though he had withdrawn the scheme, UEFA issued a letter through their lawyers in the US threatening legal action over what they had scathingly described as a "shabby, backroom, opaque deal".

READ MORE FIFA abandons World Cup privatisation plan after fierce backlash

"You and FIFA are required to take immediate steps to identify, locate, and preserve all documents and electronically stored information described in this Notice that are in your or FIFA's possession, custody, or control," its lawyer Andrew Levander said in the letter sent last Friday and seen by AFP.

Several of UEFA's member associations — Wales, Finland, Sweden and Serbia — have withdrawn their letters of support for Infantino and the English FA is strongly rumoured to be on the verge of joining them.

The scant comfort for Infantino came from a handful of supporters, including 2030 World Cup co-hosts Morocco, along with Kuwait, Qatar, where he has a house, and Lebanon, which granted him honorary citizenship in February.

The criticism only adds to the impression that Infantino has lost the confidence of even his closest FIFA collaborators.

A new challenger approaches?

Among Infantino's detractors, the hunt for a replacement has reportedly already begun.

The question now is whether his opposition can rally round one candidate with the deadline for nominations arriving on 18 November.

The name most frequently mentioned as a potential challenger or successor is Victor Montagliani, president of CONCACAF, which governs football in North and Central America and the Caribbean.

READ MORE The $28 billion plan at the centre of a growing FIFA storm

An emboldened opposition could also move sooner than that and call for an emergency meeting of the FIFA Council.

That would require the backing of 19 of the 37 members of the FIFA Council, triggering a meeting that must be held within two weeks.

In theory, the opposition has the numbers to force such a meeting, as the three confederations who were scathing of Infantino's leadership control 21 seats on the council.

European football's governing body UEFA has nine members, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) has seven, while CONCACAF boasts five.

There is another more radical option, but one that is conceivable given the backlash: a no-confidence vote in Infantino.

An extraordinary FIFA congress can be held if 20 per cent of the 211 member associations formally request it in writing.

It would take the support of just 43 member associations to spark such a move, a threshold that could easily be assembled from UEFA (55 members), CONCACAF (35) and AFC (46).

Should it come down to a leadership contest, Montagliani appears the obvious challenger as a non-European candidate. Europe has held the post since Sepp Blatter was elected in 1998.

UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin and Norway's football chief Lise Klaveness — who would be the first woman elected as president — have both ruled themselves out in the past.

title: Australians seeing record gains and losses, as 'cracks' in housing market appear
text:
Key Points A smaller number of properties made a profit in the first half of 2026 compared to 12 months prior.

Some areas experienced records gains and losses from property sales.

Property prices in Australia consistently reach record highs, but a "first crack in profitability" could signal a market downturn.

In the first half of 2026, 97.4 per cent of house resales resulted in a profit, slightly down from 97.5 per cent 12 months prior, according to new data from Domain released on Wednesday.

While it is a modest decline of just 0.1 per cent, it may indicate that the extended period of strong resale profitability is beginning to taper off.

Most people selling properties will still make "substantial gains", Domains chief residential economist Nicola Powell told SBS News.

However, the slight fall in national profitability suggests a slowing property market that could see prices fall in the future.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"While that shift is small, I think it is significant because what it's telling us is that resale profitability is a lagging indicator and tends to follow changes in home pricing," she explained.

"We've got some of our capital cities now going backward in price and particularly in some of our markets, we are seeing an increase in loss-making resales."

Source: SBS News

REA Group Senior Economic Analyst Megan Lieu said realestate.com.au data also revealed a drop in profitability.

In the past six months to July, 94.4 per cent of home resales made a profit, down from 94.9 per cent in the previous six months to January, she said.

But while properties are seeing larger average losses as profitability declines, some markets are soaring.

Where are people making and losing money on property?

While slightly fewer properties are making a profit compared to 12 months ago, successful sellers are still enjoying record returns.

Median resale profits climbed to record levels of $458,000 for houses and $237,000 for units nationally.

In the capital cities, median house profits were even higher at $552,000.

Sydney posted the country’s largest resale returns, with the median house vendor achieving a profit of $739,500.

Meanwhile, Brisbane, Perth and Adelaide are increasingly standing out as the strongest markets for seller returns, with almost every resale delivering a gain.

Source: SBS News

Perth recorded the greatest proportion of profitable house resales, with 99.6 per cent of sellers making a profit on their transaction. Brisbane led the unit market, where 99.5 per cent of resales generated a positive return.

In contrast, Melbourne remained the weakest capital city market for units. More than one in four sellers sold for less than their original purchase price, while Melbourne also recorded one of the highest shares of loss-making house resales, alongside Canberra.

Surprisingly, some areas saw both record profitability gains and losses over the year.

READ MORE The growing constituency reshaping Australian politics

Powell explained that record-high losses come from a small pool of sales.

"Those losses are perhaps large because they're in financial strife," she said.

"Or perhaps they've maybe leveraged themselves too much; they've stretched themselves too much to keep up with voracious price gains."

Home values and sale volumes fall

As overall profitability has fallen, home values and the number of properties sold have declined, according to Cotality.

In its latest report released on Monday, the group found that home values had fallen by 0.7 per cent in July and fewer people had listed their properties.

Source: SBS News

Cotality Head of Research Gerard Burg said that nationally, total home listings sat 1.1 per cent below the five-year average over the four weeks ending 26 July.

"There remains a mismatch between the pricing expectations of buyers and sellers," Burg said in the report.

"Capital city auction clearance rates have remained below 50 per cent since late May, although they have moved up from the low 40s range in mid-to-late June."

Source: SBS News

Lieu said that higher interest rates and tax changes from the federal budget are also contributing to a market slowdown.

"We expect prices to fall further in 2026, however, the extent of the decline will depend on the trajectory of interest rates and supply," she said.

A growing divide

Looking at property markets across Australia shows a "growing divide" in prices that Powell expects will continue.

On the one hand, the largest property markets — Melbourne and Sydney — are seeing prices weaken, while smaller markets in Perth, Adelaide and Brisbane continue to soar.

Source: SBS News

"Both Melbourne and Sydney are seeing an uplift in housing supply, so that increase in housing stock is giving buyers more choice," Powell explained.

While those capitals could continue to fall in price, it could be some time before other cities hit a price ceiling.

Source: SBS News

Powell said these shifts in profits and losses are normal in the property market.

"Making money off of property is about being in it for the long game," she said.

"Staying put increases your chances of actually making a healthy profit upon reselling that home, because you're riding the waves and the turns that make up the property price cycle."

title: Spain clashes with EU countries in heated talks over migration fallout
text:
In Brief Spain is feuding with regional partners following an influx of migrants into its North African territory.

Italy and Denmark have both called to suspend Spain from the EU free-travel region over the incident.

Spain's interior minister headed into a tense face-off with EU counterparts on Tuesday, as the bloc sought to draw lessons from an influx of migrants into Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta in hastily arranged video talks.

The unprecedented sight of an estimated 60,000 people streaming into Ceuta from Morocco — dozens died in the attempt and almost all have since left — exposed the fault lines on migration among EU nations.

Since images first emerged of the mass arrivals, most of whom swam around a barrier separating the enclave from Morocco, the Spanish government has found itself pitted against many of its EU partners.

The bloc's interior ministers dialled in for a videoconference that could provide a chance to look for common ground — but looked equally likely to set the stage for a showdown.

While Spain moved swiftly to send migrants back from Ceuta — where it said an estimated 2,500 remained as of Monday — the government of Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez backs a more open approach to migration than most of its EU counterparts.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Countries pushing a harder line are led most vocally by Italy — whose Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has attacked Madrid's stance, and specifically a recent push to grant legal status to undocumented migrants already in the country.

Both Italy and Denmark last week advocated suspending Spain from the Schengen free-travel area over the Ceuta crisis — a notion firmly rejected by Madrid, and which in any case is legally impossible under EU rules.

'Not a minor incident'

In a letter to the heads of the EU's institutions Saturday, Sanchez accused fellow EU countries of having "selfish" attitudes and called for emergency talks to work on a "common response" to such incidents.

Within hours, 22 countries led by Italy, Denmark, Germany and Hungary sent a counter-letter also demanding urgent talks, but with a different goal: to continue pressing their tough stance on immigration.

In a taste of what to expect, preparatory talks among the bloc's EU ambassadors on Monday saw Spain's envoy voice "frustration" with a perceived lack of support from fellow capitals, one EU diplomat told the Agence-France Presse (AFP) news agency.

READ MORE The Spanish territory at the centre of a unique migration challenge

Conversely — while all assured Madrid of their "solidarity" — some member states "are asking themselves if recent policies adopted by Spain have not sent the signal that the doors are open", added the diplomat.

The EU has significantly tightened its migration rules in recent months, including by allowing member states to send failed asylum seekers to so-called "return hubs" located outside the bloc's borders.

Italy was expected Tuesday to renew its push for the EU to set up such hubs in various African countries, on the model of an existing deal between Rome and Albania.

Rwanda and Uganda are among a dozen nations that have been scouted as potential partners to host such centres.

"I understand Spain's frustration with its failed migration policy, but we have a duty to protect Italy's borders," Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani told the Italian Corriere della Sera newspaper.

"What happened in Ceuta is not a minor incident; it poses a risk to the entire union."

READ MORE How this tiny Spanish city became a global migration flashpoint

EU heavyweight France has distanced itself from the 22-country initiative, saying it amounted to exploiting the situation in Ceuta for political ends.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has commended Sanchez's "swift handling" of the crisis, welcoming Tuesday's talks as a first step towards forging a "common European response".

The commission chief has urged the bloc to "double down" in five areas: preventing irregular migration in the first place via cooperation with partner states; strengthening external borders; implementing early warning systems; dismantling smuggling networks and reinforcing returns.

title: The concerning question around photos of a detained world leader
text:
Key Points Photographs of Aung San Suu Kyi meeting with an international aid agency have been released.

The release of the photos raised questions around the motives of the her jailors.

Photographs of Myanmar's detained former leader Aung San Suu Kyi meeting with an aid agency have been released, a visit her son described as "extremely meaningful".

It is the first independent confirmation of her condition in years as uncertainty over the health and well-being of the 81-year-old Nobel Peace Prize winner continued to grow.

Suu Kyi has been detained since February 2021, when Myanmar's military ousted her elected civilian government in a dawn coup, plunging the impoverished Southeast Asian nation into turmoil.

The whereabouts of the former head of Myanmar's pro-Democracy party, who has a large global following, have remained largely unknown since then.

Suu Kyi's son, Kim Aris, told the Reuters news agency that the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) had not been allowed to have a physician examine his mother, but said she appeared to be in good health and good spirits.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"It's the first independent proof that I've had that she's actually alive for a long time now," he said in London.

"So it's extremely meaningful."

Mon Zin, an Australian-based finance professional who fled Myanmar in the 1990s with her family, told SBS News the photos offer "relief" to her supporters.

But the release of the photographs also raises an uncomfortable question.

Why now?

Zin is the daughter of democracy activists who fled Myanmar for Australia in 1996, where she was enrolled in Year 10.

Three decades on, she is now a lawyer and regularly contributes to analysis pieces for geopolitical publications.

She told SBS News that Suu Kyi is an "admired figure" across Asia for her decades of opposing despotism in Myanmar.

"We have always admired Aung San Suu Kyi's resilience and strength. For the people of Myanmar and many in the resistance movement, when they saw the photograph, it brought them genuine relief," she said.

"It certainly did for me."

One of four photographs released by the Myanmar government showed Suu Kyi in traditional Burmese dress, standing unaided and shaking hands with an ICRC representative.

Myanmar's ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi met with Arnaud de Baecque, resident representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross. Source: AP / Myanmar President Office

Another showed the pair seated in a sparsely furnished, wood-panelled room with only two chairs and a desk.

But behind the photograph lies a much larger diplomatic campaign, she said.

"Timing is everything. Those who control when information is released often shape how it is interpreted and, in doing so, influence the narrative," she said.

So why is Myanmar's military only releasing photographs now?

"The junta chose to publicise a carefully managed humanitarian meeting with the ICRC, projecting humanitarian optics while continuing to deny political access to ASEAN, foreign diplomats and even her own family," Zin said.

"While many of us were relieved to see Aung San Suu Kyi alive, it is equally important to ask: Why was this information released at this particular moment?"

World leaders have consistently called for independent verification of Suu Kyi's well-being.

Myanmar's military-backed administrations have repeatedly claimed that Suu Kyi, daughter of Myanmar's independence hero General Aung San, is in "good health".

After a meeting between Myanmar's foreign minister and counterparts from the regional ASEAN bloc last month, Thailand's top diplomat, Sihasak Phuangketkeow, called for access to Suu Kyi.

ASEAN has barred Myanmar's leadership from its top meetings for failure to implement a peace roadmap.

Claims her charges are politically motivated

Suu Kyi has long been a proponent for human rights and democracy in Myanmar, and she was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1991.

However, she shocked the international community in 2019 when she took the stand at the International Court of Justice to defend Myanmar's military against allegations of genocide.

After a marathon run of secret trials following the coup in 2021, Suu Kyi, who was held under house arrest for a total of 15 years under a previous junta, was sentenced to 33 years' detention, convicted of charges ranging from corruption and inciting election fraud to violating state secrecy rules.

Her allies maintain that the charges were politically motivated and aimed at sidelining the most popular politician in the country of 51 million people.

The sentence was later reduced, leaving her with 18 years still to serve, according to a member of her legal team.

title: 'Free-range' eggs could face existential threat amid bird flu warning
text:
IN BRIEF Biosecurity measures are causing free-range poultry farms to move to barn-produced production.

There are 78 confirmed cases of H5 AI in Australia at present, with 58 being involved in a mass casualty event in Baudin Rocks.

The egg industry has so far remained unaffected by the H5N1 avian influenza (bird flu) outbreak; however, precautionary measures to limit the spread of the virus could drastically reduce free-range egg production.

The recent H5N1 outbreak in South Australia has sparked widespread concern for the health and safety of not only the wild bird population but also commercial farming.

Australian Eggs managing director Rowan McMonnies said the industry is "facing up to a riskier operating environment for the foreseeable future".

"Transmission between Australian wildlife indicates H5 avian influenza is established and is here to stay in the medium term," he said.

McMonnies said whilst eradication "seems unlikely", the industry has been preparing for an outbreak of this type for several years.

"Important actions are being taken to address the risks. Strict biosecurity is being maintained with enhanced measures to deter wild birds and limit crossover into egg farms," he said.

"The industry has also worked closely with authorities to improve response processes based on overseas learnings so that where farms are impacted, they can bounce back faster, limiting any impact on egg supply."

Since 2018, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) has enforced the standard that for an egg product to be considered free range it must be laid by hens that have meaningful and regular access to outdoor range during daylight, are able to roam and forage in a stocking density of 10,000 hens or less per hectare, and that the density be displayed on produced products.

However, as of July, the ACCC confirmed it won’t take enforcement action for breaches of free-range egg labelling standards due to farms choosing to house birds inside for biosecurity reasons.

'Confine birds to sheds'

Limiting free-range environments is a biosecurity measure many chicken farms are using.

"The advice is to confine birds to sheds," microbiologist and food safety expert Associate Professor Julian Cox told SBS News.

"Birds of free-ranging pick up the virus and interact — potentially spreading it to noncommercial species .... or wild birds in the vicinity could bring it into commercial poultry that are free-ranging," he explained.

Cox said it’s a measure anyone who owns and cares for poultry should consider.

"If you've got some kind of coop, lock them in the coop. It’s for their own good."

Australian egg farms are having to limit free-range farming and turn to barn-laid production in the wake of the H5 AI outbreak. Source: SIPA USA / Yevgeny Yepanchintsev

What could an outbreak mean for food safety and security?

Cox, who also serves as the scientific director of the Food Safety Information Council, said if an outbreak does occur in a commercial facility, there are processes that would be implemented to restrict its impact.

"If we start to see any sign of illness in birds .... what is likely to happen is that that flock will be destroyed, the birds will be culled," he said.

If an outbreak occurs in a region with many commercial facilities, Cox said it’s likely all birds in the "entire area" will be culled.

He said it’s a similar method to a "firebreak for bushfires".

Cox said that if a major outbreak were to occur, the "worst-case scenario" would be that thousands of birds would be culled, causing a significant supply drop in meat and eggs.

"Cleaning and restocking can take some weeks ... four to five months before flocks are replaced and producing eggs – minimum for six weeks for meat chickens," he said.

"There would be a lag in the market before we got back to the normal level of production, and that relies on the confidence that all traces of the virus are gone."

As Australia faces potential further outbreaks of bird flu, Cox reiterates that poultry meat and eggs are safe for human consumption.

"Ingesting food is not a mechanism for transmission ... it’s really about interacting with live animals," he said.

"Our food chain is so long from primary production through to purchase and consumption that it’s likely that any [sick] flocks of egg-producing birds or meat birds are going to be culled before they get anywhere near the consumer.

"We’re simply just not going to see the flu coming into our households through the purchasing of food."

title: 2026 Census: Why some Australians could go uncounted
text:
IN BRIEF The Census is compulsory for everyone in Australia on 11 August, including people experiencing homelessness.

Census field officers will visit communities, and support is available for people to complete the survey.

As day turns to dusk at Waterloo Green park in Sydney's inner south, a crowd gathers to access free haircuts, optometry and dental check-up services.

There are snags on the barbecue and one attendant tells SBS News the Homelessness Week event — dubbed Refresh, Recharge & Shine — is "fantastic".

"There should be more things like this for people in need," Marie said while assisting at the event.

NSW housing and homelessness minister Rose Jackson, who was also there on 3 August, told SBS News she believes "people don't like to think about what it's like to be homeless" but that it was important to draw the issue into the national conversation.

"Knowing how many people are living homeless, where they are, what their demographic is, their age, their gender — that's critical information for the government."

Jackson said data collected during the Census of Population and Housing on 11 August will be "crucial" for allocating resources and services to people experiencing homelessness.

But collecting this information can present logistical challenges.

"I think the ABS [Australian Bureau of Statistics] has done a really good job lifting its level of engagement. I think maybe in the past it wasn't something that was recognised as a priority," Jackson said.

"The Census was built around [dropping] a form into people's letterbox — and for people that don't have letterboxes, where do you start?"

How to complete the Census if you're experiencing housing insecurity

Sharon Callister, CEO of Mission Australia, has been working alongside Census field officers to help people experiencing housing insecurity complete the Census.

"There are rough sleepers in Sydney, and many of them are in known rough sleeping spots. Our support services staff go out there. There are also field offices coming from the Census office," she told SBS News.

She said people in temporary dwellings like boarding houses or hostels can access paper Census forms from accommodation staff.

Yolanda Saiz, CEO of the St Vincent de Paul Society NSW, says it's "critical" to ensure people experiencing homelessness are counted during the Census. Source: SBS News

Callister said it can be difficult to capture "hidden homeless" populations. That includes people sleeping in a car or tent, or couch surfing with friends, family or acquaintances without a secure lease.

"We're at a critical point in Australia. The last Census, there were [more than] 122,000 people homeless. We know from our services today that that number is going to be higher this year."

If someone is experiencing homelessness, the ABS advises people to write "NONE" in response to the question about where they usually live. Online, this question can be answered by selecting the "Elsewhere in Australia" option, then manually entering "NONE" in the suburb and locality boxes.

If a housing or homelessness service has organised and paid for a person to stay in temporary accommodation, they should write "NONE-CRISIS" for this question.

ABS spokesperson Hasan Hawatmeh told SBS Arabic that the ABS has a dedicated homelessness strategy team to support Census engagement.

"We do have a Homelessness Enumeration Week, so field staff will be deployed to do the actual enumeration. They do have access to a short form, which is a one-page [Census form] just to make sure we don't add any other complexities to the homeless population."

Yolanda Saiz, CEO of the St Vincent de Paul Society NSW, said people experiencing housing insecurity can visit the organisation's services for assistance in completing the Census.

"We can help them with computers, with access, with reading and writing if they need that help as well. So, we can facilitate their voice being captured in the Census."

The ABS is also offering in-person support at pop-up hubs and events across Australia.

Challenges in counting homelessness

In 2021, the ABS estimated that more than 122,000 people in Australia experienced homelessness at the time of the Census.

Males accounted for 55.9 per cent of this cohort, while females accounted for 44.1 per cent. Around 23 per cent of all people experiencing homelessness were aged between 12 and 24 years.

The ABS acknowledged this data may have been impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic and related restrictions.

Census field officers can be identified by their fluorescent yellow vest and ABS badge. Credit: ABS

Heidi Tucker is the CEO of Anchor, which supports people experiencing, or are at risk of homelessness. She said the Census provides "precious evidence", but believes it can be challenging to capture accurate data on homelessness, particularly in vast urban areas or in regional and rural Australia.

For regions like the Yarra Ranges in Victoria, this means locating people across more than 2,400 square kilometres, much of which is bushland.

"Not everyone who is experiencing homelessness is known to a service. We're worried that there will be people who are missed.

"We know that young people in particular can be couch surfing or living in scenarios associated with homelessness."

title: Nauru has become Naoero, the latest nation to join a growing cultural trend
text:
In brief The island of Nauru has changed its name to the Republic of Naoero.

It becomes part of a group of nations that have renamed themselves to break free from colonial-era names.

The Pacific island nation of Nauru has officially changed its name to the Republic of Naoero, reverting to its traditional designation in a move it said was intended to strengthen national identity and cultural heritage.

Nauru's parliament passed a constitutional amendment in May to rename the country, initially planning a national referendum. However, President David Adeang said in a social media post last week that the referendum plans have been dropped.

"The decision not to pursue a referendum was reached after thoughtful deliberation that Naoero is not a new name seeking acceptance by the people," Adeang said.

"It is already the identity of the people, is on the national coat of arms, and spoken in the community; and importantly is allowed by the constitution."

The abbreviated name will be "Naoero", while citizens will be referred to as "dei-Naoero".
