European colonisers changed the country's name to Nauru after finding it difficult to pronounce the island's native name Naoero.

READ MORE 'Impossible': Nauru community detainees say Australian funds not enough to buy food with

The nation is the world's third-smallest after Vatican City and Monaco, with a population of about 12,000.

Adeang said the decision was not about politics but about identity, heritage, and "preserving the legacy of our ancestors and strengthening the future of our children".

The government has formally notified international organisations and countries of the change, with the transition process already underway.

A more meaningful name

Over the last 50 years, nations asserting their independence from former colonial empires have led to a growing trend — national name changes.

For many nations like Naoero, the desire to revert to their original pre-colonial names is about cementing a sense of national identity or pride.

Timor-Leste adopted its current name — a Portuguese tautology in which both words mean "East" — in 2002. It was previously known as Timor Timur — its Indonesian name that, funnily enough, also meant "East East" — from 1975 until independence.

Tuvalu and Kiribati took back their names in 1978 and 1979 respectively, doing away with colonial names the Ellice Islands and Gilbert Islands.

Vanuatu followed suit in 1980, retiring the name New Hebrides after becoming independent.

Overseas, Türkiye was among the most recent major nations to change its name.

Its campaign for a name change started in 2021 when Turkish president Recep Erdoğan began asking various international bodies to observe the traditional spelling and pronunciation.

Erdoğan felt that the name Türkiye represented "the culture, civilisation and values of the Turkish nation in the best way".

In 2018, Eswatini retired the name Swaziland to mark the 50th anniversary of Swazi independence. The name means "land of the Swazis" and was chosen, in part, to avoid being confused with Switzerland.

Cabo Verde, recently rising to fame for their underdog run in the 2026 FIFA World Cup, officially ended use of the name Cape Verde in 2013.

The change came about after national delegates asked the United Nations to use only Cabo Verde for official purposes rather than the Anglicised version.

Namibia did away with the name Southwest Africa in 1990, while the Republic of Côte d'Ivoire changed from the Ivory Coast in all official capacities in 1986, and has refused to acknowledge any translation of its name from French ever since.

Burkina Faso retired the name Upper Volta in 1984 in favour of combining two words from local languages — "Burkina" (from Mooré, meaning "upright") and "Faso" (from Dyula, meaning "fatherland"). Other translations note its meaning as "land of the honest/incorruptible men".

In 1980, Zimbabwe dropped Rhodesia from its name, one coined by colonialists two decades earlier.

In 1975, the Republic of Dahomey became Benin, and Dutch Guiana became Suriname.

title: The growing constituency reshaping Australian politics
text:
The ongoing housing crisis is having severe repercussions on individuals and families in Australia. It has limited young people’s ability to move out, increased the rate of involuntary lifelong renting, and pushed vulnerable populations into homelessness.

These are not the only changes that flow as a result of housing unaffordability. Our new research demonstrates it’s also reshaping how people vote.

An interesting case study

A longstanding body of academic work links individuals’ assets to their political and ideological beliefs, including the parties they vote for.

This literature shows people with more valuable assets are more likely to hold right-leaning political beliefs. They are also more likely to support conservative parties that favour the status quo over efforts to redistribute money and wealth more equitably throughout a society.

For the average person, the family home is the most valuable asset they will ever own. However, surprisingly few studies have considered the influence of home ownership on voting preferences. Australia represents an interesting case study for two key reasons.

First, Australian major political parties differ in their electoral positions regarding housing policy. In particular, the Coalition of the Liberal and National parties has historically favoured homeowners through — for example — negative gearing and tax discounts. In contrast, since the 2010s, the Australian Greens and the Labor Party have progressively adopted more pro-renter stances.

Second, Australia’s trend towards housing unaffordability is particularly pronounced by international standards. This is reflected in increased home and rental prices, reduced homeownership rates and increased property-ownership concentration. This situation creates a greater divide in the economic interests of renters and homeowners, potentially shifting (or entrenching) party preferences.

Our research

Our new study explored how housing tenure relates to voting behaviour in Australia. We also wanted to know whether the relationship has become stronger over time.

We analysed survey data from more than 19,000 people participating in ten iterations of the Australian Election Study between 1996 and 2022. The Australian Electoral Study interviews people shortly after each national election, collecting information on their demographic traits, economic position and sociopolitical attitudes.

READ MORE How Australian housing became a generational budget battleground

We analysed these survey data to examine associations between individuals’ self-reported housing tenure and the party they voted for in the last election. We also kept other relevant factors constant, such as age, income, area of residence and social class.

The ‘homeowner, conservative voter’ association

In a first set of analyses, we compared the voting preferences of renters, mortgage holders and outright owners, pooling data from 1996 to 2022.

All else being equal, there is a clear link between home ownership and voting for the Coalition. Specifically, 45.6 per cent of outright owners voted for the Coalition, compared with 44 per cent of mortgage holders and 37.6 per cent of renters.

By contrast, 34.2 per cent of outright owners, 36.3 per cent of mortgage holders, and 38 per cent of renters voted Labor.

In other words, there is a pro-Coalition advantage of 11.4 percentage points among outright owners, and a smaller 7.7 percentage-point advantage among mortgage holders when compared to Labor. For renters, however, we observe a slight Labor advantage of 0.3 percentage points.

The analyses also unveiled interesting patterns for the Greens, who disproportionately attract renters. In fact, our data indicate 23 per cent of Greens votes come from renters, compared with just 11 per cent and 18 per cent for the Coalition and Labor, respectively.

Together, these results align with the premise that the Coalition has been historically successful in attracting homeowners as a key constituency.

They also suggest that having a mortgage makes people more likely to vote for policies that redistribute wealth and provide a buffer against interest rate changes.

Renters, on the other hand, visibly lean towards parties that more actively support tenants’ economic interests.

Are things changing over time?

Importantly, our research shows the influence of home assets on voting behaviour is not static. Rather, it has changed visibly over the 26 years between 1996 and 2022, aligning with the increasing cost of living and housing.

Crucially, the data show renters have progressively abandoned the Coalition as their party of choice. While 44 per cent of renters voted for the Coalition in 1996, just 31 per cent of renters did so in 2022.

READ MORE Home prices fall across Australia as housing downturn takes hold

On the aggregate, these voters seem to have been absorbed for the most part by the Greens, who saw the share of renters voting for them increase from 3 per cent in 1996 to 20 per cent in 2022.

How might future elections look?

Our study provides evidence that homeownership should be a factor to be considered in its own right in analyses of political behaviour, separate from other asset types.

The findings reveal a strong and increasing tendency for renters to vote for left-leaning over right-leaning parties. This could have significant implications for both future election results and party strategies, especially as renters account for an increasing share of the adult population.

At the same time, renters have seen their market power deteriorate, further motivating them to find a party or candidate committed to helping them. Parties that design policies to appeal to renters may therefore reap rewards in future elections.

If the current trend extends into the future, renters may indeed hold the key to reshaping the Australian political landscape.

Francisco Perales is an adjunct professor at the School of Government and International Relations at Griffith University.

Ferran Martinez i Coma is a professor of political science at Griffith University.

title: 'Unfounded and premature': Why experts say parents shouldn't panic about screen time
text:
IN BRIEF An international study of more than 3,000 children found no link between the amount of screen time and developmental difficulties at ages five or 10.

Experts note the study began in 2009 and the technology children have access to now has evolved.

Concerns about children and screen use may be overblown, new research suggests, with experts saying worries about an 'iPad baby' generation may be "premature".

A new international study, based on data from over 3,000 children, found no link between screen use duration and developmental difficulties at ages five or 10.

Researchers in the UK spoke with the families of children back in 2009 and 2010 and followed their development for the subsequent 10 years.

Over that time, there has been some criticism and debate about the role of technology in parenting, and whether young people born in the 21st century will be a screen-addicted generation.

The iPad was released in Australia in 2010, and a child growing up around this time is sometimes referred to as an 'iPad baby'.

While the findings are limited by self-reported survey data, Australian experts say the results counter popular messaging about parenting and technology.

"Fear from parents around screen time is unfounded and premature," Associate Professor David Armstrong from the School of Education at La Trobe University told SBS News.

"It's really a mixed bag over whether there are any adverse effects on kids' development, and it's good to note that there are some advantages of devices for social development."

READ MORE Social media companies not asking for proof of age despite higher penalties

He described the findings as "robust and methodical", saying they contribute to an emerging body of research calling not for less screen time, but for better use of it.

But Professor Andrew Whitehouse, an autism researcher at The Kids Research Institute Australia, said the findings should be taken with a grain of salt, as young children in 2026 have access to more smart devices than in 2009.

"The saturation of childhood by these devices came in the years afterwards," he said in a statement.

"This means that across early childhood, the children had almost no exposure to the ubiquity of smart devices as now exists."

As content increasingly targets children and is designed to maximise viewing time, experts say the best tools parents have are managing content and ensuring quality time away from screens.

Good vs bad screen time

Screen time is not inherently harmful said Adam Guastella, a clinical psychologist who works with Sydney Children's Hospital at Westmead and the University of Sydney.

Rather, the effects on a child's physical, cognitive and social development come down to content.

"If you're doing the same thing repetitively over and over and over again, in terms of cognitive development, that's not going to be good. Particularly if what you're practising doesn't have any functional significance," he told SBS News.

However, technology can provide opportunities for growth.

"You want children being exposed to opportunities for learning and challenges and problem solving; you want them to be learning information that's going to help them to develop skills," he explained.

On average, Australian children aged five to 17 spend two hours and 51 minutes per day on sedentary recreational screen activity, according to data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) released in June.

READ MORE Big tech companies could be hit with higher taxes if they don't strike deals with publishers

In this way, only one in four Australian children meet national health guidelines, which recommend no more than two hours of sedentary recreational screen time per day, excluding homework.

Guastella said screen time and the opportunities technology offers, such as socialising or education, should be balanced by in-person connections and physical activity.

If a child is missing milestones or exhibiting antisocial behaviour, it could be less about screen time itself and more about the loss of time for other activities like reading and playing, he said.

Children's content is changing

The three main categories of a child's "screen diet" are typically television and streaming, gaming and social media, according to the Australian Institute of Family Studies.

But as newer generations of parents switch from living room screens to tablets and smartphones, the kind of content their children consume could shift as well.

Dr Sam Teague, an NHMRC Emerging Leadership Senior Research Fellow at James Cook University, said today's technology is more targeted at younger children though is typically aimed at engaging them rather than educating them.

"The content is not developed and moderated with children's development in mind, and the algorithms recommending videos are based on maximising watch time rather than what's best for children," she said in a statement.

Today's children aren't just consuming a different type of screen time — the total amount of time they spend on screens has also been rising over the years.

But while television and video games have been studied for decades, there is less evidence on newer technologies such as smartphones and algorithm-driven social media.

"We may see different outcomes for today's five-year-olds than those in this study, and we need more research like this tracking children today to see how they grow and develop in today's digital environments," she concluded.

Other factors could be more important

While harms around screen time should still be debated, Armstrong said there's conclusive evidence on some of the main causes of poor childhood development.

"Poverty is a huge determinant of a child's success, and the adverse effects of poverty are much more established than tech, yet they are rarely discussed," he said.

READ MORE The new plan to prevent data centres from driving power prices up

"Kids experiencing poverty and marginalisation consistently have poorer outcomes, yet we focus a lot of policy debate on social media and tech."

Armstrong said that children with disability and those from diverse backgrounds also tend to experience worse social, behavioural and physical outcomes.

"That’s not to say that screen time or social media aren’t harmful at all, but the large amount of discussion of them is disproportionate to the impact."

title: 'Steadfast advocate': Arnhem Land's Rirratjingu clan elder Bakamumu Marika dies
text:

A respected elder of Arnhem Land's Rirratjingu clan, Bakamumu Marika AM, has died, the clan group's Aboriginal corporation has announced.

title: Big tech companies could be hit with higher taxes if they don't strike deals with publishers
text:
In brief New laws could see tech giants hit with higher taxes in Australia.

Companies like Meta and Google would need to strike deals with news publishers on content use.

Tech firms will pay a higher levy or strike more deals to avoid the charge under planned tweaks to an initiative to force them to hand over some of their revenue to media companies.

The proposed news bargaining incentive will push companies like Google, Meta and TikTok to strike commercial deals with news organisations to use the publishers' content on their platforms.

If deals are struck, the companies will pay a smaller share of their Australian advertising revenues to the government than if they refuse to reach agreements.

The levy will apply to tech giants with domestic revenues of $250 million or more, with any funds raised to be redistributed to the media sector.

But after a consultation period on the changes, which Labor hopes to legislate when parliament returns in Spring, elements of the incentive have been tipped further in favour of news publishers.

title: Home prices fall across Australia as housing downturn takes hold
text:
In brief National home prices fell 0.7 per cent last month, the biggest monthly drop since December 2022.

Sydney and Melbourne led the falls, while top-end homes lost 3.2 per cent over three months.

Australia's housing market downturn is spreading across the country as higher interest rates and changes to property taxes take hold.

Figures from property analytics company Cotality showed national home prices fell 0.7 per cent last month, the largest single-month decline since December 2022.

Annual growth has slowed to 5.3 per cent, well below the double-digit pace recorded earlier this year.

The country's largest property markets, Sydney and Melbourne, recorded declines of 1.4 per cent and 1.2 per cent respectively. Both cities are more than five per cent lower than recent peaks.

Brisbane and Adelaide, where prices have recently boomed, also recorded drops of 0.6 and 0.2 per cent respectively.

In Perth, which has recorded the strongest year-on-year growth of any capital city at 21.8 per cent, prices were virtually flat, rising just 0.1 per cent.

"For buyers who remain in the market, lower competition and elevated stock levels (when compared with the start of the year) mean greater choice and more negotiating power," the property analytics firm said.

However, the fall in prices has been led by properties at the higher end of the market, providing little benefit to first home-buyers who are also grappling with lower borrowing capacity after three interest rate hikes this year.

Homes in the top quarter of the market lost 3.2 per cent of their value in the three months to July, compared to a 0.3 per cent gain in the lower-price tier.

Beyond the capital cities, the regional property market recorded a drop a 0.2 per cent — the first decline since January 2023.

"There remains a mismatch between the pricing expectations of buyers and sellers," Cotality head of research Gerard Burg said.

Consumer sentiment has also been soured by high living costs, uncertainty caused by the ongoing Middle East war and tax changes announced in the May budget.

"We have observed a deterioration in the flow of new listings across the country in recent weeks, led by Sydney, as potential vendors assess a weak market and choose to wait until conditions improve," Burg said.

Rental prices have continued to rise due to low vacancy rates. Burg said national median rents had risen by more than $200 a week in the last five years.

"Despite the tight market conditions, there are question marks about how much further rents can rise," he said.

There’s something about this remote spot close to the western edge of the vast Sahara Desert that feels eerily familiar. I’m standing in a historic fortified village made entirely of rammed earth, clay, straw and wood that towers high above the dusty plains and valley below. Everywhere around me, in all directions, are crumbling networks of winding paths leading ever upwards, and one large flat arena, all brushed the same muted hue of old burnt toffee. A Berber man in front of the historic wooden gate of Ait Benhaddou. iStock I’ve never been to this part of Morocco, along the old caravan route between the Sahara and the fabled ancient market city of Marrakesh, and have never even heard anything about it. So why on earth do I have this strange sensation that I know it well? Then I spy a tiny restaurant along one of the spider web of alleyways. It’s called Gladiator. Two doors down is a souvenir stall, selling photographs from the TV drama Game of Thrones.

Advertisement

And, finally, it sinks in. This tiny 11th-century corner of North Africa with its intact 17th-century structures might be virtually unknown to most of us, but it’s been seen on screen by billions of people worldwide. That’s as the site where Maximus Decimus Meridius, played by a young Russell Crowe, fought for his life to enact vengeance on his enemies, and where Daenerys Targaryen marched up to the earthen walls with her army to free the slaves. Sign up for the Traveller Deals newsletter Get exclusive travel deals delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up now. Ait Benhaddou – the village that launched a thousand movies. iStock So, of all the gin joints, in all the towns, in all the world – to quote Humphrey Bogart in Casablanca, another classic set just 420 kilometres north of here – Ait Benhaddou in southern Morocco is one of the oldest, and best-preserved complete ksars (fortified villages) on earth, and one that could comfortably stand in for any ancient empire facing dark days. For today’s set-jetting tourists – those who love to visit the places where their favourite films were shot – this place glows head and shoulders over its cinematic rivals. The UNESCO-listed mud-brick citadel, topped with a granary from which there are magnificent 360-degree views, has inspired everyone who’s visited, and continues to inspire all those who watch the films and TV series that have been shot here.

Advertisement

And that’s all the way back to scenes in the 1962 epic Lawrence of Arabia, and all the way forward to this year’s mega-hit The Odyssey, directed by Christopher Nolan. Yes, of course. Where else could honestly look such a fitting ancient backcloth for Homer’s classic poem? Admiring the landscape around Ait Benhaddou. iStock In between, there have been some scorchers – The Man Who Would Be King, starring Sean Connery and Michael Caine in 1975; The Jewel of the Nile, with Michael Douglas, Kathleen Turner and Danny DeVito in 1985; and Martin Scorsese’s The Last Temptation of Christ in 1988. There’s The Mummy from Brendan Fraser and Rachel Weisz in 1999; Ridley Scott’s Kingdom of Heaven in 2005 with Orlando Bloom; and even Nicole Kidman got to stay for the 2015 Werner Herzog film, Queen of the Desert. But standing there, in this still-intact slice of the old world, its rugged paths worn by millions of footsteps over the centuries, its ancient walls constructed using medieval methods and designed to repel all invaders, its small homes still inhabited by several families … It’s a stunning glimpse of life from a long-ago age.

Advertisement

“Filmmakers love coming here,” says local man Mohamed Elmekke. “There is so much for them to see, and it looks just as it did when it was first built so many centuries ago. And we, over all that time, have been enjoying working as extras!” Berber carpets on display on the market streets in historic Ait Benhaddou. iStock As we speak, a steady stream of visitors start the walk from the modern village next door over the bridge across the river to the citadel and then to ascend the long paths spiralling around the ksar to the top. For anyone visiting Morocco, this is an absolute highlight. And with the flood of overseas visitors expected to come to Morocco for the 2030 FIFA World Cup – co-hosting with Spain and Portugal – it’s likely to become much better known, too. THE DETAILS

The ritual hoisting of your carry-on bag into the overhead bin on a Jetstar flight? Come February, you’re going to have to pay for the priority to put your bag there. Jetstar announced today it will reduce passengers’ free carry-on allowance to a single item, down from two, and begin charging a fee for guaranteed access to overhead bin space. Unpaid carry-on items will still be permitted in the overhead compartments, but only after the cash-paying priority travellers get first dibs. Jetstar passengers are now being forced to compete in the carry-on Hunger Games. Jetstar is changing its policy for carry-on baggage. What’s galling is that the “new product” – access to the overhead bin – was formerly a standard product. Jetstar’s marketing is a sleight of hand, of sorts. As consumer advocate Adam Glezer notes: “You’re not paying for a bin. You’re paying for a better chance at one.”

Advertisement

Related Article Aviation New consumer protections would undermine Jetstar’s ‘existence’: CEO It’s the same plane, same lockers, with nothing added, said Glezer, of Consumer Champion. “They’ve made free space scarce and now charge you for a headstart.” It’s also a reminder that getting on a plane headed for Bali (nearly synonymous with the Jetstar brand) provides little respite from the reminder of inequality (extra fees, priority boarding, The Chairman’s Lounge) that somehow make the experience of the cost-of-living crisis worse. Perhaps for this reason, when asked about Jetstar’s change, Victoria’s newly minted premier, Ben Carroll, gave a revealing comment, suggesting almost a resignation with the airlines. While he opposed Jetstar’s new fee, Carroll said: “Having been with my family on a Jetstar flight recently, can I say I’m not surprised?

Advertisement

“It was hard enough getting on and having to pay for your coffee and everything else,” Carroll told ABC radio. And yet, as Jetstar was quick to point out, they didn’t come up with the idea of charging for priority access to the overhead bins. Loading This is unfortunately the norm in Europe, where the profitable airlines are the cheapest. Ireland-based Ryanair, which does a booming business, developed, under chief executive Michael O’Leary, a business model that establishes that if you want anything more than your seat, you have to pay extra. Jetstar seems to be heading down the same path.

Advertisement

UNSW senior aviation lecturer Ian Douglas said the new Jetstar fee is “pretty much consistent with all the carriers in Europe”. Douglas said that for many European airlines, the airfares don’t cover total operating costs. “It’s the ancillary revenues from bags, seat assignments, loyalty programs that get the total industry to profit.” Ancillary fees for baggage and seat selection made up almost a third of Ryanair’s €15.54 billion ($25.5 billion) revenue in the past financial year. Ancillary revenue share ranges from a mere 3 per cent for full-service carriers to 62 per cent for ultra-low-cost airlines, according to airline retail and revenue strategy company IdeaWorksCompany, quoted in Forbes. It will be cold comfort that Qantas-owned Jetstar occupies a unique place as one of the few successful low-cost carriers owned by a national premium carrier.

But as the cheapest in Australia, it also advocates for low levels of customer service. Chief executive Steph Tully recently said the aviation consumer protections being legislated are “a prescriptive one-size-fits-all” solution that “to be honest, would undermine Jetstar’s existence”. External discussion of Clarkson’s position and future has included the fact that Adam Simpson and John Longmire – both Kangaroos playing greats who went on to coach AFL premierships at other clubs – are not presently employed as senior coaches. Clarkson’s contractual terms, however, were negotiated in his favour back in 2022, when Essendon were interested in appointing him to replace Ben Rutten. He had just had a season’s sabbatical after Hawthorn paid him out $900,000, the final year of his deal with the Hawks, to expedite the handover to Sam Mitchell. North Melbourne, which has received the highest amount of variable funding from the AFL of Victorian clubs over the past two years (surpassing St Kilda which had long held that mantle), has been a relatively frugal club since the 2000s, having wiped off its debt and repeated financial benefits from their stint of playing home games in Hobart and now Western Australia.

title: Burning billions: SpaceX’s sales are soaring, but its spending even more so
text:
Advertisement

BusinessCompaniesElon Musk Opinion Burning billions: SpaceX’s sales are soaring, but its spending even more so Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist August 5, 2026 — 12:05pm

August 5, 2026 — 12:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There was something very familiar about SpaceX’s first quarterly result as a listed company. A near-doubling of revenue was swamped by a massive increase in spending. After initially soaring more than 9 per cent on the result, SpaceX shares gave up all its gains as investors digested the rate and scale of the increase in capital expenditures, which dwarfed the 92 per cent jump in sales to $US7.8 billion ($11.1 billion). It’s not just spaceships that rocket at SpaceX, with its investments in AI going through the roof. Getty SpaceX’s capex leapt from $US2.8 billion in the same quarter last year and $US10.1 billion in the March quarter to a whopping $US18.4 billion, with the company flagging it will remain at about that same rate for the rest of the year. That would mean capex of about $US65 billion this year. While SpaceX isn’t a pure artificial intelligence play – it also has its profitable Starlink satellite business and its unprofitable Starship rockets – that broad narrative of explosive revenue growth being overwhelmed by the scale of investment is consistent throughout the AI sector.

Advertisement

Critical to the fate of AI, or at least of those US companies pursuing their costly proprietary advanced AI models, is whether the trillions of dollars they are investing will ever generate a return commensurate with that investment and its inherent risk. At this point in the sector’s development, that remains an open question. Revenue from AI is up about 250 per cent. But the capex driving that revenue growth is up by more than 550 per cent. SpaceX is generating revenue growth beyond market expectations, including growth in its AI revenues, which have risen from $US737 million in the June quarter last year to $US818 million in the first quarter of this year and then to $US2.6 billion in the latest June quarter. So, revenue from AI is up about 250 per cent. But the capex driving that revenue growth is up by more than 550 per cent. Moreover, SpaceX’s sales growth isn’t coming purely from selling AI products to customers, but rather from selling access to its AI infrastructure. The company is selling “compute” – processing power – to Google for $US920 million a month, and to Anthropic for $US1.25 billion a month.

Advertisement

As for the rest of the AI sector, the future for SpaceX’s AI business is cloudy, with the only near-term likelihood that its losses – $US1.26 billion in the latest quarter and $US2 billion for the first half of this year – will continue to mount. Related Article Opinion

Sharemarket Brave new world: SpaceX is now the most expensive stock on the planet Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Elon Musk, of course, remains super confident. He says he expects the “cadence” of AI development to improve dramatically and the company to end this year with 2GW of capacity and “closer to 10GW of compute than 5GW of compute” next year. He also believes SpaceX’s overall revenue base is about to explode. The June quarter revenues, annualised, produce a run-rate of just over $US30 billion for the financial year. By 2030, he says, he expects revenues to reach $US1 trillion – a year earlier than his earlier projections. Indeed, there was a “non-zero probability” that the $US1 trillion mark could be achieved in 2029, he said.

Advertisement

To get there by 2030 – which would require an annual compound growth rate in revenues of about 140 per cent – AI will have to be central for the company, but it won’t all be about AI. The only profitable business in SpaceX’s portfolio at this stage is its Starlink satellite business, which had revenue of $US4.3 billion (up from $US2.6 billion a year earlier) and generated a profit of $US1.66 billion. Starlink now has 12 million subscribers, double the level of a year ago. That satellite business might soon be complemented with a wireless service, which will send shudders through the senior ranks of AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile, whose share prices all fell on the news. SpaceX said it will acquire spectrum and build the terrestrial infrastructure that will enable Starlink to offer a direct-to-mobile service. As for the rest of the AI sector, the future for SpaceX’s AI business is cloudy, with the only near-term likelihood that its losses will continue to mount. Critical to Musk’s vision of data centres in space and the colonisation of Mars (and strengthening Starlink’s coverage and capabilities) is the space business, in which SpaceX invested $US1.2 billion during the quarter, and which generated revenue from its Starship launches of $US962 million.

Advertisement

Starship’s giant reusable rockets, while having had a troubled gestation, would dramatically reduce the cost of launching payloads, and people, into space and are the key to SpaceX’s ability to build those orbiting data centres, powered by the sun, and eventually putting people on Mars. SpaceX, which launched two Starship V3 test flights earlier this year, says Starship “continued to advance towards full and rapid reusability.” Elon Musk’s SpaceX is burning through cash. AP The underlying questionmark over all Musk’s ambitions is whether he will run out of cash before he realises them. The cash burn at SpaceX is significant and accelerating. The initial public offering in June, which raised about $US85 billion, may have left the group with net cash of $US93.5 billion, but the AI and Starship programs will rapidly diminish that cash pile.

Advertisement

There have been reports that Musk is considering the sale of Tesla’s China operations as a prelude to a merger of SpaceX and Tesla, which has more than $US40 billion of cash, but Musk wasn’t drawn on the merger question in the analyst briefing for SpaceX’s results. There is, however, a significant amount of overlap between SpaceX and the increasingly AI-centric Tesla, and the market expects Musk’s two listed vehicles to eventually merge. Whether that would resolve, or at least delay, a need for new SpaceX funding is uncertain, given that Tesla, too, is significantly ramping up its capex and spending on AI. While most of the analysts who follow SpaceX (many of whom work for banks involved in the IPO) remain wildly bullish about SpaceX’s prospects – and SpaceX did beat almost all their forecasts, other than their big miss on capex – the wider market is a little less certain. Shares in the IPO were offered at $US135 each and, post-listing, initially soared to $US225. They closed at about $US125 on Tuesday, before tumbling more than 8 per cent – at one point they were down by about $US11 a share – after the market closed. SpaceX has lost more than $US1 trillion of market value from its peak.

Advertisement

And there may be more losses to come. On Thursday in the US, about 911.5 million shares that were in lock-up before the quarterly’s release, will be available for trading. Related Article Opinion

AI Scared by tech’s debt deluge, investors are questioning the AI boom Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist That compares with the 640 million currently available, accounting for roughly 5 per cent of SpaceX’s issued capital. It could have been even more, had SpaceX shares continued to trade at elevated prices, with the release of a further 455 million dependent on the company hitting share price thresholds. The 911.5 million shares are a giant over-hang on the shares, and short-sellers have been queuing up in anticipation, with positions equivalent to more than a third of the shares currently available for trading. While the IPO’s aftermarket might have been disappointing – and costly, for those who subscribed to the IPO, who could still face a rocky few days, weeks or months – SpaceX still has a market capitalisation of about $US1.7 trillion.

Advertisement

That is pretty impressive for an unprofitable, capital-devouring company and an indicator of the market’s faith in Musk, his fantastical visions and the eventual (and necessarily unprecedented, given the sheer scale of the investments) profit-generating potential of AI. title: Libertarian MP demands ICAC hearing be halted, calls for inquiry into ‘leaking’

A NSW MP has called for the Independent Commission Against Corruption’s bombshell examination of illegal donations to be paused pending an inquiry into whether the watchdog has been leaking information to the media. John Ruddick, a Libertarian Party member of the NSW upper house, claimed in parliament on Wednesday that Operation Rosny “appears to be tainted” because the Herald has revealed several details about the key players targeted by the ICAC over recent weeks. Ruddick wants the Inspector-General of the ICAC, Gail Furness, SC, to investigate whether ICAC staff had disclosed information in a potential breach of the law, and also demanded parliament order an independent inquiry into his claims. He offered no evidence to support his allegations, other than that the Herald’s coverage has referenced sources who are unauthorised to speak publicly.

Advertisement

The ICAC began its investigation in mid-2022 into the links between the NSW Liberal Party, fugitive Sydney developer Jean Nassif, Catholic Schools NSW and several other figures, including from the Labor Party. Operation Rosny is due to hold eight weeks of public hearings. Related Article Live

Operation Rosny ICAC Operation Rosny LIVE updates: Jean-Claude Perrottet begins evidence as inquiry enters eighth day Ruddick is particularly focused on a story by the Herald late last month which revealed names on the witness list for the first week of hearings. Ruddick has repeatedly suggested on social media platform X that the ICAC staff leaked the document. However, the witness list was widely circulated to parties involved in Operation Rosny before the Herald obtained and published the document. Ruddick told parliament it should condemn “any attempt by a financially desperate, taxpayer-supported media organisation to weaponise confidential ICAC processes or interfere with the integrity of public hearings for its own commercial or political ends”.

Advertisement

He cited stories from more than a decade ago to support his claim the Herald has used confidential sources to report on matters involving the ICAC. On July 30, a solicitor for the ICAC, Roy Walden, emailed Ruddick to say it had been made aware of “comments by you on X, in which you alleged that ‘operatives within the ICAC are leaking to the SMH on an industrial scale’.” Walden said in his email that he was not aware of any evidence that any commission officer has “leaked” information in relation to Operation Rosny. Walden also said if Ruddick had any evidence of misconduct by ICAC staff it should be referred to Furness in her capacity as the inspector of the ICAC. Meanwhile, Jean-Claude Perrottet, the 29-year-old brother of former premier Dominic Perrottet, told the commission on Wednesday he was “let go” from his job at Catholic Schools NSW in June, just one month after being promoted.

Perrottet, a key member of the right-wing Catholic group the Reformers which is at the centre of the corruption inquiry, confirmed he was made redundant from the education body just weeks before Operation Rosny was announced. Catholic Schools NSW chief executive Dallas McInerney is also a person of interest to ICAC. Jean-Claude Perrottet gives evidence at the corruption inquiry. ICAC This commission is investigating whether Jean-Claude Perrottet solicited unlawful donations from prohibited donors. One of those was hotelier Michael O’Hara. It is also probing whether McInerney approved donations from Catholic Schools NSW to the Liberal Party, via the Reformers. “I want to suggest to you, Mr Perrottet, that the reason you were made redundant only a month after you’ve been promoted to this new role was because of your involvement in this inquiry. Is that right?” counsel assisting Juliet Curtin asked Perrottet. “That wasn’t what was communicated to me from the office and the emails that I received. But I mean, obviously, I’ve thought about the timing of it,” he responded.

Senior NSW Liberal MP Damien Tudehope conceded on Tuesday he had leaked a confidential draft report from a parliamentary inquiry to a key witness who deliberately avoided giving evidence, in a stunning revelation that could threaten the party elder’s political future. Tudehope, then the Coalition government’s most senior member of the upper house, sent the 2023 confidential report into illegal donations and the Hills Shire Council to lobbyist and Liberal Party operative Jeremy Greenwood, the Independent Commission Against Corruption heard on Tuesday. Greenwood was one of four Liberal apparatchiks who hid or fled overseas to avoid being handed a summons to appear before the parliamentary inquiry, which was one of the catalysts for the broader ICAC probe. title: Victoria Hannan’s marriage ended at 28 with a text message. It marked a new beginning
text:
Advertisement

LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life Victoria Hannan’s marriage ended at 28 with a text message. It marked a new beginning Victoria Hannan August 5, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I separated from my husband not long after Eat Pray Love came out. By the time the divorce was finalised a year later, I had, against my will, acquired three copies of Elizabeth Gilbert’s divorce memoir. One arrived anonymously in the mail. Two others were slid across cafe tables by friends who looked at me with the sort of expression people usually reserve for the recently bereaved. If you’re one of the few who missed the Eat Pray Love phenomenon, the premise was simple enough: God comes to Elizabeth Gilbert on the floor of her bathroom after hours of praying and gives her the confirmation she needs to leave her husband, so she destroys her marriage and reconstructs herself overseas. Italy for appetite. India for spirituality. Bali for love. When she divorced at 28, author Victoria Hannan felt a freedom, but also a powerful uncertainty. This kind of drama is the lifeblood of a divorce narrative: marriage-ending equals world-ending. There’s also a factoid that people quote with alarming solemnity: that divorce, moving house and death are life’s three greatest stressors. My own divorce, however, felt less like catastrophe and more like admin. There were no lawyers. No custody arrangements. No dramatic division of money or real estate. I was 28 years old and our shared assets amounted to one large IKEA saucepan and a collection of Curb Your Enthusiasm DVDs.

Advertisement

I got the saucepan. We had been together since we were 20. Married for four years. The marriage did not end because anybody committed some unforgivable act. It ended because somewhere along the way I began to feel fixed in place. I remember worrying too much about the wedding gifts. Would his old boss want the juicer back? At 27, I had started to feel as though I was trapped inside an earlier version of myself. The person I had been at 20 was still making decisions for me. There were things I wanted to do, ways I wanted to live and selves I wanted to try on. I could not work out whether growth inside a marriage was possible when the marriage itself had been built when we were so young. Now that I’m in a healthy relationship that supports change, I know this growth is possible. But at 27, I lacked the language for any of this.

Advertisement

Nobody tells you how to get divorced, especially when so young. We were the first of our friends to marry and both our sets of parents were still together. We had no earthly idea what was supposed to happen next. (I’ve often thought there should be a small bureaucratic clause in your marriage certificate: In the event of dissolution, do not panic. This happens all the time!) My reference points for divorce were Elizabeth Gilbert and Elizabeth Taylor: one made divorce appear spiritually transformative, the other made it look glamorous. Mine was neither. Nothing was dramatically wrong. My husband was kind. There was no betrayal, no event I could pinpoint to justify dismantling a life. If anything, this just made the divorce feel faintly embarrassing. Julia Roberts played Elizabeth Gilbert in the film version of Eat Pray Love. We had stood in front of our friends and families and announced, with absolute confidence, that this arrangement would last forever. Then, four years later, our pledge was quietly redacted. I remember worrying too much about the wedding gifts. Would his old boss want the juicer back? At the time, this seemed as pressing a concern as the emotional collapse of the marriage itself.

Advertisement

By the time we officially separated, we were already living in different cities and leading separate lives with increasing competence. The divorce itself happened almost entirely via paperwork in Australia while we were living in the UK. Nobody appeared in court. At one point, my ex-husband phoned someone to confirm the paperwork had gone through, then he texted me. And that was that. A marriage over in a text message. Related Article Sunday Life Five years after I had a ‘COVID baby’, these words from a psychologist still break me Afterwards, I found myself trying out different performances of a young divorcee. My instinct was to make a joke of it by referring to it as my “first divorce”, like it was no big deal. But it was a big deal. It was desperately sad, and it made me feel ashamed. I had made a public declaration and then failed to uphold it. But as time passed – and my therapy sessions increased – I was able to start to reframe it. What if the divorce was not the tragedy? What if the tragedy had been remaining exactly where I was? Because with the shame came a powerful sense of uncertainty (and hope) about the shape the future held. Suddenly, I felt free from the exhausting pressure of trying to force permanence onto something that no longer fit. I felt relief from the idea that staying was inherently more virtuous than leaving.

Advertisement

We tend to see marriage as success and divorce as failure because culturally we remain deeply invested in endurance as a moral achievement. But sometimes ending a marriage is the hopeful act.

I didn’t speak to God, I didn’t go to an ashram or have my life changed by a plate of spaghetti. What I experienced instead was quieter. It was the sense that my life had become, once again, unwritten. And with my pen in hand, I was ready to start again. I Love the Whole World! title: Stokes on booze, Baz, next year’s Ashes and his ambition to coach England
text:
Advertisement

SportEngland Stokes on booze, Baz, next year’s Ashes and his ambition to coach England Will Macpherson August 5, 2026 — 11:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Key points Former England cricket captain Ben Stokes told his former teammates Stuart Broad and Jos Butler on their podcast that he doesn’t believe his team had a drinking problem, but he does think the sport’s relationship with alcohol has not moved with the times.

The all-rounder dismissed suggestions he would return to the England Test team as a player, but said he wanted to one day coach his country.

Stokes said he was surprised his vice-captain Harry Brook was not appointed as his replacement as Test captain and had concerns about his good friend Joe Root returning to the role.

The podcast heard Stokes wrote an uncommissioned report into England’s dismal Ashes campaign last Australian summer.

Stokes also spoke about his relationships with outgoing Test coach Brendon McCullum and England cricket director Rob Key.

Ben Stokes believes cricket’s relationship with alcohol has not “moved on” as the game has become more professional but denied the England team he captained had a drinking problem. Stokes ended a 15-year international career in June when his Test side lost to New Zealand, but is continuing to play for his boyhood county Durham. England captain Ben Stokes leaves the field at Trent Bridge after his final innings. Getty Speaking in-depth for the first time since retiring in Nottingham, Stokes appeared on For The Love of Cricket, the podcast hosted by his friends and former teammates Stuart Broad and Jos Buttler. Stokes was asked directly by Broad if his team had a drinking problem, following a series of late-night episodes over the past year, headlined by Harry Brook being punched by a bouncer in Wellington, hours before captaining England in an ODI before the Ashes.

Advertisement

Stokes refuted the allegation: “No … that is such an extreme thing to put on a team. “But I think cricket has a drinking culture and that has not changed. We are in 2026 now, where the game has gone more professional over the years. But one thing that has just stayed within cricket is its relationship with alcohol, from club cricket it works its way up. It stays there and is embedded within the sport. Loading “That is the relationship between alcohol and cricket, it has not moved on as the game has become more professional. There’s more science and medicine, more nutritional information, more this and that. One thing that has been a constant, and has been for a very long time, is the relationship with alcohol. For people who think the English cricket team has a drinking culture, I would say no. I would just say cricket has a culture that is associated with alcohol.” Stokes has had an up and down relationship with alcohol across his career. In 2017 he was arrested for a brawl in Bristol while drunk after an ODI against West Indies, was found not guilty of affray and later gave up alcohol. After England beat New Zealand at Lord’s in June, he went out and was accused of breaking the team’s curfew.

Advertisement

“I think it [cricket’s relationship with alcohol] can be a problem,” he said. Related Article England Bazball apology: McCullum owns up for failed England experiment “If you look at everything over the years, a lot of people who have been involved within cricket, have had bad relationships with alcohol. I don’t know what you do to change it. It’s just one of those things that … I have had, I don’t want to say problems, but I’ve had relationships with alcohol over my career that have been potentially dangerous, if that makes sense. But that is completely different to me now. “There is a relationship with alcohol that has been the same since the 1980s, as the game has got better and better, that has stayed around.” However, Stokes said he did not regret his decision to take his team for a mid-Ashes trip to the Queensland seaside resort of Noosa last summer, despite scrutiny of their drinking there.

Advertisement

Ashes prospects There has been much speculation, including from managing director Rob Key, that Stokes could return for next year’s Ashes. He has continued to shut this down, and described himself as “definitely” retired. Stokes also spoke about how, aged 35, he could not envisage playing on under another captain, unlike his predecessors Root and Alastair Cook, who were both 31 when they stepped down from the captaincy. The snubbing of Brook Root has already done a five-year stint as captain before Stokes, but has been installed alongside the new Test coach, Stephen Fleming. Brook will remain in charge of the white-ball side with Brendon McCullum as coach. Key, the managing director, said the Test role had come “too soon” for Brook, who is 27.

Advertisement

“I think just if you think someone’s going to be a good captain or a good leader, then just give them it,” Stokes said. “Brooky was made vice-captain – I’m not there any more, but even when I missed that Test match, I was like: ‘He’s vice-captain?’ I sort of understood the reasoning why they were saying it, but what message is that sending to him? Ben Stokes thought his deputy, Harry Brook, should’ve assumed the England capataincy once he retired. ECB via Getty Images “He’s vice-captain, and the captain is not playing, but he’s not captain. And then the same again here [with the permanent role].” Stokes expressed concern about Root, a close confidant, doing the job after the toll it took during his first stint between 2017 and 2022.

Advertisement

“I love Rooty and I wish him nothing but success,” he said. “I hope he achieves amazing things in his role as captain. He’s going to really enjoy working with Flem. He’s a great man, I’ve worked with him before. I told Joe, I said my only worry is just you. “And that’s all I really care about now, just because I have seen what he went through and how much he put himself through [last time as captain]. “He’s just always put the team first, like he always comes second. And that’s just my only concern with it is just obviously knowing what he went through last time he was in charge of the team because I don’t want to see that ever happen again because I care for Joe a lot, but I wish him all the success in the world.” Coaching ambitions

Advertisement

Stokes has taken tentative first steps in coaching in the Hundred, with England Lions and the Durham academy, but has set his sights on coaching England. “I’m doing my level three coaching [course] now while I’m still playing because I want, when the day comes that I’m not playing any more, I’d love to be able to have all that stuff signed off and done,” he said. “I know what I want to do in terms of staying within the game, which is to be a coach. “And would I love to be coach of England one day? Absolutely. I just really like the idea of being in some form of leadership away from playing.” Ben Stokes has returned to his county, Durham, since retiring from international duty. Getty Images England’s Ashes review

Advertisement

Stokes confirmed that he provided a written a review of England’s Ashes campaign, despite not being asked for an official report. “I just found it interesting and weird that maybe that’s never happened before,” he said. “Maybe a captain’s never really been [asked], ‘can you give us your official [thoughts]’ ... so I was like, stuff it, I’m going to do anyway. I was writing stuff down.” Ben Stokes and Brendon McCullum led the England Test team for four years. Getty Images He said his wife, Claire, and mother-in-law helped him write the report and he made sure it was right “in terms of structure and spelling” because “I didn’t want to do it half-a---- because it was such a big thing for me”. The response was a “good meeting” with Key and McCullum, who all remained in their job initially. Six months on, only Key survives. Stokes expressed surprise that McCullum was sacked as Test coach, saying his relationship with the coach remained strong despite reports of tactical divergence during the Ashes.

Advertisement

Related Article Exclusive

Australian cricket ‘Pretty annoying’: Inside Josh Hazlewood’s fight to keep his Test career alive When it came to the Rex Rooms incident that he admits contributed to the end of his career, Stokes said he was “not here to go into all that detail”. He described it as a “sticky situation for quite a few people involved”. “There’s a time and a place for that,” he said. “And now isn’t that time because I don’t want to come across bitter towards anyone yet because I’m chilled right now.“

title: Secret missions and staged meetings: How a backroom deal led to IBAC probe
text:

Updated PoliticsVictoriaIBAC Secret missions and staged meetings: How a backroom deal led to IBAC probe Kieran Rooney Updated August 5, 2026 — 11:55am ,first published August 5, 2026 — 9:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. An eight-year-long investigation into negotiations between the Andrews government and the firefighters’ union has found “serious and concerning conduct” by Victorian ministers, MPs and public servants. The findings were contained in Operation Richmond, an investigation led by the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission (IBAC) that began in 2018, and which was suppressed for years by legal challenges, despite the watchdog’s efforts to have it made public. Operation Richmond centred on dealings between Daniel Andrews’ government and the United Firefighters Union under Peter Marshall. Marija Ercegovac Tabled in parliament on Wednesday, the IBAC report identified serious issues in the way pay deals with the Country Fire Authority (CFA) and the Metropolitan Fire Brigade (MFB) were negotiated alongside the establishment of Fire Rescue Victoria. However, it stopped short of finding corrupt conduct – for which Victoria has a higher threshold than any other state. “IBAC found that senior members of government acted contrary to established policies, procedures, codes of conduct and conventions in negotiating a deal with the secretary of the United Firefighters Union [UFU], Mr Peter Marshall, for the CFA Enterprise Bargaining Agreement [EBA] without the knowledge and involvement of the responsible minister, agencies and department,” Commissioner Victoria Elliott said at the start of the report.

Advertisement

“By doing so, the government placed itself in a position where Mr Marshall was able to exert extraordinary influence over the negotiations for both the CFA EBA and the MFB EBA.” The report covers a period when Daniel Andrews was premier of Victoria. The CFA pay deal became a political flashpoint for his government, and the late Jane Garrett resigned as emergency services minister and quit cabinet because she disagreed with her government’s moves to accept UFU demands. “The government placed itself in a position where Mr Marshall was able to exert extraordinary influence.” Delayed Operation Richmond report “During the period investigated, IBAC also found that Mr Marshall was afforded privileged access to senior members of government which, in many cases, were not disclosed and were to the exclusion of other key stakeholders,” the report said. “Operation Richmond highlights how government leaders, including ministers and the premier, can undermine established checks and balances when they fail to model high integrity standards and act as stewards of good governance.”

Advertisement

The report was originally scheduled for release by the end of June, but was delayed by an unsuccessful legal challenge from Marshall. Related Article IBAC Firefighters’ union boss loses court battle to bury corruption investigation, but appeal possible Operation Richmond began after IBAC received allegations that Marshall had blackmailed or compromised the premier to change his position on the 2016 CFA pay deal. The blackmail claim was never substantiated. The investigation was widened to include negotiations for a pay deal with the Metropolitan Fire Brigade and the creation of its replacement, Fire Rescue Victoria. Ultimately, it found that in 2016 Andrews authorised then special minister of state Gavin Jennings, with the assistance of Tony Bates – a deputy secretary at the Department of Premier and Cabinet – to negotiate the CFA deal directly without the knowledge of the CFA themselves.
